guides.title: How to Hire a Roofer in Arizona | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: How to hire a roofer in Arizona: check the ROC license, bonds and insurance, get written estimates and contracts, and spot storm chasers and red flags.
guides.h1: How to hire a roofer in Arizona
guides.lead: A roof is one of the largest purchases most homeowners make, and the contractor matters as much as the materials. Here is how to check a roofer out before you sign anything.
guides.answer: To hire a roofer in Arizona, confirm an active Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC) license at roc.az.gov, ask for proof of liability and workers' compensation insurance, and get a detailed written estimate and contract. Avoid anyone who asks for a large cash payment up front, pressures you to sign that day, or cannot give you a local address.

sections.h2: Start with the ROC license lookup
sections.body:
In Arizona, contractors who do roofing work for pay generally must be licensed by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors. The ROC runs a public lookup at roc.az.gov where you can search by business name, license number or the name of a qualifying party. It takes a couple of minutes and it is the single most useful check you can make.

When you pull up a license, look at more than whether it exists. Check that the status is active, that the business name matches the name on the estimate, and that the license classification covers roofing. Residential roofing is typically licensed under a residential roofing classification (R-42) or a dual residential and commercial classification (CR-42). A general handyman or a landscaping license is not the same thing.

The lookup also shows the license history and any complaints that went through the ROC process. One old, resolved complaint on a long-running business is not unusual. A pattern of recent complaints, suspensions or a license issued last month under a new name deserves more questions. Our license is ROC #096629, and we encourage every homeowner to look it up.

sections.h2: Bonds and insurance: what each one does
sections.body:
Licensed Arizona contractors carry a license bond, which the ROC requires as a condition of the license. A bond is not insurance for your house. It is a limited pool of money that can help a homeowner if a contractor fails to follow the law or the contract. Homeowners who hire a licensed residential contractor may also have access to the Arizona Residential Contractors' Recovery Fund, which exists for valid claims against licensed residential contractors. Hiring an unlicensed roofer generally leaves you outside that protection.

Insurance is separate. Ask for a certificate of general liability insurance, which covers damage the crew causes to your property, and proof of workers' compensation, which covers injuries to workers on your roof. Roofing is physical work at height, and if an uninsured worker is hurt at your home, you do not want that to become your problem. A legitimate contractor will have the certificates sent directly from their insurance agent.

sections.h2: Get a written estimate you can compare
sections.body:
Every bid should be in writing and should describe the actual work, not just a total. A useful estimate names the roof area, the material and color, whether the old roof is being removed, the underlayment type, how damaged decking will be handled, flashing and vent work, permits, cleanup and the warranty. Two estimates that look far apart are often describing different jobs.

Our guide to reading a roofing estimate walks through each line item. For a general sense of what drives cost, see the Roofing Cost Guide. Every roof is different, so a real number only comes from looking at your roof.
Ask the same questions of each contractor so the answers are easy to compare. Write the answers down, because a good contractor will be happy to put them in the estimate or contract.
bullets: What is your ROC license number, and who is the qualifying party?
Can your insurance agent send me certificates for liability and workers' compensation?
Will your own crew do the work, or do you subcontract it?
Who will be my point of contact during the job, and how do I reach them?
What underlayment and flashing will you use, and is that written in the estimate?
How do you handle rotted decking or other surprises once the old roof is off?
Will you pull the permit, and who schedules the inspections?
What does the workmanship warranty cover, for how long, and is it in writing?
How do you protect my landscaping, pool and driveway, and how do you clean up nails?

sections.h2: What a good roofing contract includes
sections.body:
The contract turns the estimate into an agreement. It should list the contractor's legal name, address and ROC number, the full scope of work, materials by brand or specification, the price, how change orders are handled, the payment schedule, the expected start window and the warranty terms. Read the warranty language closely, including what voids it.

Change orders matter on roofs because some problems, like soft decking, only show up during tear-off. A fair contract explains how hidden damage will be priced, for example as a set rate per sheet, and says the contractor will show you the damage before charging for it. Do not sign a contract with blank spaces, and keep a signed copy for your records.

If you sign a contract at your home after a salesperson comes to your door, federal and Arizona rules generally give you a short window to cancel. The contract should explain your cancellation rights in writing.

Reasonable payment terms tie money to progress. A modest deposit to schedule the job or order special materials is common, with the balance due at milestones or on completion. Be cautious about paying most of the job before any work starts, and never pay a large amount in cash to someone you cannot verify.

Pay by check or another traceable method, get a receipt for every payment, and make payments to the business named on the license rather than to an individual. Before the final payment, walk the job with the contractor, confirm the permit inspection passed, and make sure cleanup is done. Ask whether the contractor provides lien releases from material suppliers, which helps protect you if a supplier is not paid.

Most cities in the Phoenix area require a permit for a roof replacement and for many larger repairs, and the city inspects the work. Rules differ between Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Phoenix and other cities, so ask your contractor what your city requires. The licensed contractor normally pulls the permit, and the permit should show their name and license number.

A roofer who asks you to pull the permit yourself as an owner-builder, or who says a full replacement does not need one, is shifting responsibility onto you. Permits protect you when you sell the house, too, since buyers and inspectors may ask about unpermitted work.

sections.h2: Storm chasers and other red flags
sections.body:
After a big monsoon storm, out-of-state crews often arrive in Arizona neighborhoods, knock on doors and offer fast roof replacements paid by insurance. Some are legitimate, but many are gone by October, which makes warranty service difficult. A local contractor with a physical office and a long history is easier to hold to a promise.

Watch for these warning signs before you sign:
bullets: No ROC license, a license under a different name, or a license that is not for roofing.
Pressure to sign today, or a deal that expires when the salesperson leaves.
Requests for a large cash payment up front.
An offer to cover or waive your insurance deductible, which can be insurance fraud.
A bid far below the others with a vague, one-line scope.
No local address, only a cell phone number and an out-of-state plate.
Asking you to sign over your insurance claim before they have inspected the roof.

sections.body:
Integrity Roofing has been family owned and operated since 1993, with one office in Gilbert at 16308 E Fairview St. We are licensed, bonded and insured under ROC #096629. When we look at a roof we explain what we see, show photos, and put the scope in writing so you can compare it with any other bid. Read more about us or see our roof inspections.

To schedule an estimate, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: How do I check a roofer's license in Arizona?

Go to roc.az.gov and use the contractor search. Look up the business name or license number, then confirm the license is active, the name matches your estimate, and the classification covers roofing work.
Does a roofer in Arizona need a license?

Generally yes. Arizona requires contractors to be licensed by the Registrar of Contractors for roofing work, with only narrow exceptions for very small jobs. A roof replacement or significant repair should always be done by a licensed contractor.
What is the difference between a bond and insurance?

A license bond is a limited amount of money tied to the contractor's license that can help if the contractor violates the law or contract. Liability insurance covers damage the crew causes to your property, and workers' compensation covers injured workers. You want a contractor with all three.
How many roofing estimates should I get?

Two or three detailed written estimates is usually enough to understand the scope and the range. More important than the number is making sure each estimate describes the same work so the comparison is fair.
How much should I pay up front for a new roof?

A modest deposit is common, with the rest tied to progress or completion. Be wary of anyone who wants most of the money before work begins, and always pay with a traceable method to the licensed business.
Is it a red flag if a roofer offers to cover my deductible?

Yes. Offering to waive or absorb your insurance deductible can amount to insurance fraud, and it often signals a contractor who plans to cut corners elsewhere. A reputable roofer will not make that offer.
Who pulls the roofing permit?

In most cases the licensed contractor pulls the permit and schedules the city inspection. Be cautious if a roofer asks you to pull it yourself, because that can shift responsibility for the work onto you.
How can I tell if a roofer is a storm chaser?

Storm chasers often arrive right after a big storm, knock on doors, push for quick decisions and lack a local office or Arizona history. Check the ROC license date and business address, and favor contractors who will still be around for warranty calls.

guides.title: Tile Roof Underlayment in Arizona | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Why tile roof underlayment fails before the tile in Arizona heat, the warning signs, how a lift-and-relay re-felt works step by step, and material choices.
guides.h1: Tile roof underlayment in Arizona: what it is and when to replace it
guides.lead: Concrete and clay tile can last for generations, but the layer underneath does the real waterproofing, and Arizona heat wears it out much sooner.
guides.answer: Tile roof underlayment is the waterproof layer beneath the tiles that actually keeps water out of your home. In Arizona, heat and UV break it down long before the tile wears out, so many tile roofs need a lift-and-relay, also called a re-felt, where the tiles are removed, new underlayment is installed, and the same tiles are put back.

sections.h2: What underlayment does on a tile roof
sections.body:
Tile is a water-shedding surface, not a watertight one. Wind-driven rain and runoff get under and between tiles, especially at overlaps, valleys and around penetrations. The underlayment is the membrane that catches that water and carries it down to the edge of the roof and out of the house.

On a typical Arizona tile roof, the layers from the bottom up are the roof deck, the underlayment, battens or tile fasteners, flashing at walls, valleys and vents, and then the tile. If the underlayment fails, the tile can look perfect from the street while water reaches the deck below. That is why a tile roof that looks fine can still leak.

sections.h2: Why underlayment fails before the tile in Arizona
sections.body:
Concrete and clay tiles are very durable. The underlayment beneath them is made of asphalt-saturated felt or synthetic material, and it lives in an oven. On a summer afternoon in the Valley, the space under the tile gets far hotter than the air temperature, and the roof goes through that heating and cooling cycle day after day for months.

Over years, that heat drives oils out of traditional felt, and it becomes dry, brittle and cracked. Wherever tiles are cracked, slipped or missing, the underlayment is also exposed to direct UV light, which speeds up the damage. Foot traffic from solar installers, pest control, holiday lighting or satellite work can crack brittle tiles and tear aged felt beneath them.

The result is a pattern many Arizona homeowners discover the hard way: the tiles still have decades of life left, but the waterproofing under them is worn out. How long underlayment lasts depends on the material, the installation, the roof pitch and how much sun the roof gets, which is why an inspection is more reliable than a calendar.

sections.h2: Signs your underlayment may be failing
sections.body: Some signs show up inside the house, some from the ground, and some only when a roofer lifts a few tiles to look. Common ones include:
bullets: Water stains on ceilings or walls, especially after monsoon storms or winter rain.
Leaks that return after spot repairs, often in valleys or near walls.
Cracked, slipped or missing tiles that leave the underlayment exposed to sun.
Dark, brittle or crumbling felt visible at the eaves or under a lifted tile.
Granules or black debris washing out of gutters or onto the patio.
Daylight or stains on the roof deck when you look in the attic with a flashlight.
A roof that is roughly the age of the house and has never been re-felted.

sections.h2: The lift-and-relay (re-felt) process step by step
sections.body:
A lift-and-relay replaces the underlayment and reuses your existing tile. Because the tile stays, the finished roof looks much the same as before, and the existing tile does not have to be hauled off. Here is how the job usually goes:

  1. Inspection and scope. We look at the tile, the underlayment, flashing and the deck, and write up what will be replaced, including how broken tiles and damaged decking will be handled.
  2. Permit. Where the city requires it, the permit is pulled before work starts.
  3. Remove and stack the tile. The crew lifts the tiles in sections and stacks them on the roof or staged nearby, sorting out any that are broken.
  4. Tear off the old underlayment. Old felt, battens and worn fasteners come off down to the deck.
  5. Inspect and repair the deck. Soft, rotted or delaminated sheathing is replaced so the new system has a sound base.
  6. Install new underlayment. The new membrane is laid with proper overlaps, starting at the eaves and working up.
  7. Flashing and details. Valleys, wall and pan flashings, vent pipe flashings and drip edge are replaced or reset as the scope calls for.
  8. Battens and tile. Battens go back where the system uses them, and the tiles are relaid and fastened, with replacement tiles where needed.
  9. Ridges, hips and cleanup. Ridge and hip tiles are set, debris is hauled away, and the yard is checked for nails before final inspection.

sections.h2: Underlayment types: felt vs synthetic, 30# vs 2-ply
sections.body:
The underlayment spec is one of the most important lines in a re-felt estimate, so it is worth knowing the common options.

30# felt is traditional asphalt-saturated organic or fiberglass felt. It has a long track record, but a single layer is the most vulnerable to Arizona heat over time.

2-ply or double-layer systems use two layers of felt, often a base sheet and a heavier cap sheet, so there is a second line of defense if the top layer cracks. Many Arizona tile roofs use some version of a two-layer system.

Synthetic underlayments are woven or spun polymer sheets that are lighter, tear resistant and generally more stable under heat and UV than felt. Some are rated specifically for high-temperature tile applications. Quality and heat ratings vary between products, so the brand and product name should be on your estimate.

The right choice depends on your roof, your tile profile, manufacturer requirements, local code and your budget. Ask each contractor which product they plan to use and why, and see our tile roofs page for more on how we work with concrete and clay tile.

Some tiles break during removal and reinstallation no matter how careful the crew is, and some are already cracked from foot traffic or age. A good estimate explains how replacements are handled, for example whether a set number of replacement tiles is included and how additional tiles are priced.

Replacement tiles come from a few sources: matching new tile if the profile and color are still made, salvaged tile from other jobs, or borrowing tiles from a less visible area such as a back slope and using the closest available match there. Moving original tiles to the street side keeps the front of the house uniform.

Many Phoenix-area neighborhoods have HOAs with rules about roof color and tile profile. Because a lift-and-relay reuses most of your existing tile, it usually keeps the roof looking the same, but any replacement tiles still need to blend in. Check with your HOA before work starts in case they require a review or approval, even for a re-felt.

If your tile profile has been discontinued, you may need HOA approval for the closest match or for a full change of tile. We can provide product information to help with that request. Learn more about our roof replacement services or call 602-548-3770 to schedule an inspection. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: What is a tile roof re-felt?

A re-felt, also called a lift-and-relay or underlayment replacement, is when the tiles are removed, the old underlayment is replaced with new material, and the existing tiles are put back. It renews the waterproofing without replacing the tile itself.
How long does tile roof underlayment last in Arizona?

It depends on the material, installation quality, roof pitch and sun exposure. Traditional felt tends to wear out much sooner than the tile above it in Arizona heat, so an inspection is the best way to know where your roof stands.
Can I just replace the broken tiles instead?

Replacing broken tiles helps protect the underlayment from sun, but it does not fix underlayment that is already brittle or torn. If leaks keep returning after tile repairs, the underlayment is often the real problem.
Is synthetic underlayment better than felt?

Synthetic underlayments are generally lighter, more tear resistant and more stable under heat and UV than single-layer felt. Product quality varies, so ask for the specific brand and its heat rating, and compare it with a two-layer felt system.
Will my roof look different after a lift-and-relay?

Usually very little, since the original tiles go back on. Any replacement tiles are matched as closely as possible, and original tiles can be moved to the front of the house so the most visible slopes stay uniform.
Do I need HOA approval for a re-felt?
Some HOAs require approval for any roof work, while others only care about changes in tile color or profile. Check your HOA rules before scheduling so the project is not delayed.
How long does a lift-and-relay take?
The time depends on roof size, complexity, deck repairs and weather. Your contractor should give you an expected schedule in writing and tell you how they protect the open roof if rain is forecast.
Is a re-felt cheaper than a full tile replacement?

Reusing the existing tile usually means less material and less disposal than replacing everything. Every roof is different, so see our Roofing Cost Guide for the factors that affect cost and get a written estimate for your home.

guides.title: Monsoon Roof Prep Checklist for Arizona Homes | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Arizona monsoon roof checklist for June 15–September 30: what to do before, during and after storms, how to spot damage from the ground, and when to call.
guides.h1: Monsoon roof prep checklist for Arizona homeowners
guides.lead: Arizona's monsoon brings dust, wind, sudden downpours and hail. A little preparation before the season and a careful look after each storm can keep small problems from becoming leaks.
guides.answer: Arizona's monsoon season runs June 15–September 30. Before it starts, have your roof inspected, clear debris from valleys, gutters and scuppers, and fix loose tiles or flashing. After each storm, look for damage from the ground, check the attic and ceilings for leaks, photograph anything you find, and call a licensed roofer for anything beyond simple cleanup.

sections.h2: Why monsoon season is hard on roofs
sections.body:
The National Weather Service defines Arizona's monsoon season as June 15–September 30. Storms during these months often arrive fast, with strong outflow winds, blowing dust, heavy rain over a short time and sometimes hail. A roof that handles a slow winter rain fine can struggle with a sudden downpour pushed sideways by wind.

Monsoon storms also follow months of intense heat. By June, aged underlayment, dried sealants and cracked tiles are at their most vulnerable. Flat roofs with clogged scuppers can pond water quickly, and debris that sat quietly all spring gets pushed into valleys right when they need to carry the most water.

sections.h2: Before the season: May and early June
sections.body: The best time to prepare is before the first storm. Spring gives you time to schedule repairs before roofers get busy with storm calls. Work through this list:
bullets: Schedule a professional roof inspection so cracked tiles, worn flashing and soft spots get fixed before storms hit.
Clear leaves, palm fronds and debris from gutters and downspouts, using a stable ladder or a pro.
Make sure flat roof scuppers and drains are open and that water has a clear path off the roof.
Trim tree branches that hang over or rub against the roof.
Check that vent pipes, skylights and roof-mounted equipment are sealed and secure.
Look for slipped or broken tiles and missing shingles from the ground with binoculars.
Secure patio furniture, umbrellas, trampolines and anything that can blow onto the roof.
Take dated photos of your roof and ceilings now, so you have a before record if you need to file a claim later.

sections.body:
Most monsoon leaks we see start where water collects or changes direction. Valleys are the channels where two roof slopes meet, and they carry a lot of water in a short time. When leaves, dust and tile fragments pile up in a valley, water backs up and can run sideways under tile or shingles and over the edge of the flashing.

Flat roofs and low-slope sections depend on scuppers and drains, the openings that let water off the roof through the parapet walls. A scupper clogged with a nest, a ball or a drift of leaves can turn a flat roof into a shallow pool during a heavy storm. Standing water finds every weak seam. Ask your roofer to clear valleys and scuppers as part of a spring visit, especially if you have trees nearby. Learn more about flat roofing and foam roofs.
Stay off the roof and away from ladders during storms. Lightning, wind and wet surfaces make a roof dangerous, and no leak is worth a fall. Here is what you can do safely from inside:
bullets: Watch ceilings near exterior walls, skylights and vents for new stains or drips.
If water is coming in, move belongings, put down towels and set a bucket under the drip.
If a ceiling bulges with water, keep people away and avoid touching wet light fixtures.
Note the time and what the storm was like, such as heavy wind or hail, for your records.
If wind or water threatens electrical service, turn off power to that area only if it is safe to do so.

sections.h2: After the storm: what to check from the ground
sections.body: Once the storm has passed and it is daylight, walk around the house and look up. You can see a lot from the yard, the street or a second-story window, and binoculars help. Do not climb onto a wet or damaged roof. Look for:
bullets: Tiles that are cracked, slipped out of line or missing, or shingles that are lifted, creased or gone.
Pieces of tile, shingle or granules on the ground, in gutters or on the patio.
Bent or loose flashing, vent caps or drip edge.
Tree limbs or debris resting on the roof.
Dents or spatter marks on gutters, patio covers or AC units that suggest hail.
On flat roofs, water still standing a day or two after the storm, or blistered coating.
Inside, new ceiling stains, peeling paint, damp insulation or a musty smell in the attic.

sections.body:
Good records make insurance conversations and repairs go more smoothly. Start as soon as it is safe and before anything is cleaned up or repaired. Take wide photos that show the whole side of the house, then close-ups of each damaged spot. Photograph interior stains with something for scale, and keep pieces of broken tile or debris.

Write down the date and time of the storm and what you noticed. Keep receipts for anything you spend to prevent further damage, such as a tarp or water cleanup, since many policies expect you to take reasonable steps to limit damage. Read your policy or call your agent about how claims work, and get a written assessment from a licensed roofer. Our damaged roof page explains how we handle storm damage repairs.

Big monsoon storms bring door-to-door roofing crews into Valley neighborhoods. Before you let anyone on your roof or sign anything, look up their license at roc.az.gov and ask for a local address. Be cautious with anyone who offers to cover your deductible or wants you to sign over your claim on the spot. Our guide on hiring a roofer in Arizona has a full list of red flags.

Call a licensed roofer if water came into the house, if you see missing or broken roofing material, if flashing is loose, if a flat roof is holding water, or if hail was large enough to dent metal around the house. Even small damage is worth a look during monsoon season, because the next storm may only be days away.

We repair monsoon and storm damage across Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Phoenix and the East Valley. Call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. See our repairs and maintenance services for more.

faqs: When is monsoon season in Arizona?
The National Weather Service defines Arizona's monsoon season as June 15–September 30. Storm activity varies from year to year, but planning around those dates gives you a clear window to prepare.
When should I get my roof inspected before monsoon?
Spring, roughly March through May, is ideal. That leaves time to schedule any repairs before the first storms arrive and before roofers get busy with storm calls.
Can I clean my own gutters before monsoon?

Many homeowners can safely clean gutters from a stable ladder on a single-story home. Walking on tile or steep roofs is risky and can crack tiles, so leave on-roof work and two-story ladders to a pro.
What should I do if my roof leaks during a storm?
Stay off the roof. Move belongings, catch the water with buckets and towels, and keep away from bulging ceilings or wet fixtures. Once the storm passes, photograph the damage and call a roofer.
How do I know if my roof has hail damage?
From the ground, look for cracked tiles, bruised or missing shingles, granules in gutters, and dents on gutters, patio covers and AC units. A roofer can confirm hail damage up close.
Should I put a tarp on my roof after a storm?
A tarp can limit further water damage, but climbing a wet or damaged roof is dangerous. If you are not comfortable on a ladder and roof, have a roofer handle temporary protection when it is safe.
Why does my flat roof hold water after monsoon storms?
Clogged scuppers or drains, low spots or sagging areas can keep water from draining. Water that stands more than a day or two can damage the roof surface, so it is worth having a roofer check it.
What photos should I take for an insurance claim?

Take wide shots of each side of the house, close-ups of damaged roofing, gutters and other items, and photos of interior stains. Note the date of the storm and keep receipts for any emergency protection you paid for.

guides.title: Arizona Roof Maintenance Calendar | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: A month-by-month Arizona roof maintenance calendar: spring inspections before monsoon, summer heat care, fall checks and winter rain prep, DIY vs pro tasks.
guides.h1: Arizona roof maintenance calendar: month by month
guides.lead: Arizona roofs face a predictable year: mild spring, extreme summer heat, monsoon storms, a calm fall and winter rain. Matching your maintenance to that cycle keeps small issues small.
guides.answer: In Arizona, plan a professional roof inspection in spring before monsoon season, keep debris cleared through summer, check for storm damage after each monsoon, and do a fall check before winter rains. Homeowners can safely handle ground-level checks, gutter cleaning on single-story homes and attic inspections, while on-roof work and repairs should go to a licensed roofer.

sections.h2: How Arizona's climate shapes roof care
sections.body:
Most roof maintenance advice is written for places with snow, ice and long rainy seasons. Arizona is different. Our roofs deal with intense UV and long stretches of heat, followed by the monsoon season from June 15–September 30, and then lighter winter storms. Heat and sun age materials, while short, heavy storms test them.

That means the most important maintenance happens before monsoon season, and the most important check happens right after it. The calendar below follows that rhythm. Dates are guides, not rules, and a roof with known problems may need attention sooner.

sections.h2: What you can safely do vs what a pro should do
sections.body:
A lot of roof care can happen from the ground or the attic. Walking on a roof is a different story: tile cracks under feet, foam and coatings can be damaged, and falls from roofs cause serious injuries. Here is a simple way to split the work.

Homeowner tasks:

  • Look over the roof from the ground with binoculars after storms and each season.
  • Clean gutters and downspouts on a single-story home from a stable ladder.
  • Trim small branches you can reach from the ground.
  • Check the attic with a flashlight for stains, daylight or damp insulation.
  • Watch ceilings for new stains and keep dated photos.
  • Keep a simple file of inspections, repairs and warranty paperwork.

Pro tasks:

  • Walking the roof and replacing cracked or slipped tiles.
  • Resealing or replacing flashing, vent boots and skylight seals.
  • Clearing valleys and flat roof scuppers on the roof surface.
  • Inspecting and repairing underlayment, foam or coatings.
  • Any work on a two-story roof or a steep slope.

sections.h2: January and February: winter rain check
sections.body:
Winter storms in the Valley are usually gentler than monsoon storms, but they last longer, and slow steady rain finds worn underlayment and cracked sealant. After a winter storm, check ceilings and the attic for new stains. Note any drips and their locations, since winter leaks often point to problems that will get worse in summer.

This is also a good time to review last year's records. If you had repairs during monsoon season, look at those areas again from the ground.

sections.h2: March and April: schedule the spring inspection
sections.body:
Spring is the best time of year for a professional roof inspection. The weather is mild, roofers have more open schedules than in late summer, and there is time to fix problems before the heat and storms. A roofer can check tile, flashing, underlayment edges, sealants, vents and flat roof surfaces up close.

On your end, clear gutters and downspouts of winter debris, trim branches that hang over the roof, and take a fresh set of dated photos of each side of the house.

sections.h2: May and early June: finish repairs before monsoon
sections.body:
Use May and the first half of June to complete any repairs from the spring inspection. Have valleys and scuppers cleared, loose tiles reset and flashing sealed. If your roof has a foam or coated surface, ask whether it is due for a recoat. Our monsoon roof prep checklist covers this period in detail.

Secure patio furniture, umbrellas and anything else the wind can lift, and make sure you know where your insurance policy and roofer's phone number are.

During monsoon season, the main job is watching and responding. After each significant storm, walk around the house and look for cracked or missing tiles, lifted shingles, debris on the roof, loose flashing and pieces of roofing in the yard. Check the attic and ceilings for new stains.

Summer heat matters too. Avoid having people walk on the roof in midday heat, when materials are hottest and most easily damaged. If you plan to add solar, holiday lighting brackets or anything else on the roof, ask the installer how they protect tile and seal penetrations.

  • Photograph any damage right away, before cleanup.
  • Call a licensed roofer for anything beyond debris on the ground.
  • Clear gutters again if a storm loaded them with debris.

Once monsoon season ends, do a full walk-around and attic check. Storm damage does not always leak right away, and a cracked tile from August can turn into a winter leak. If you saw anything suspicious over the summer, fall is a good time for a roofer to take a closer look while the weather is comfortable.

Fall is also a sensible time to plan larger projects. If an inspection shows the underlayment is near the end of its life, the cooler months are a good window for a tile underlayment replacement or other major work.

sections.h2: December: get ready for winter rain
sections.body:
Before winter storms, clear leaves from gutters and downspouts, especially if you have deciduous trees that drop late. Make sure downspouts direct water away from the foundation. If you put up holiday lights, use clips that do not require nails or screws in the roof, and avoid walking on tile to hang them.

Wrap up the year by updating your roof file with any inspections, repairs and photos. Good records help with warranty questions, insurance claims and selling your home.

sections.h2: Let us handle the on-roof work
sections.body: We provide roof inspections, repairs and maintenance for tile, shingle, foam and flat roofs across the East Valley and Phoenix area. To schedule a spring inspection or a post-monsoon check, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: How often should I have my roof inspected in Arizona?
Once a year is a good baseline, ideally in spring before monsoon season. Add a check after any major storm or if you notice a leak or damaged material.
What is the best month for roof work in Arizona?
Spring and fall are usually the most comfortable and practical months, with mild temperatures and fewer storms. Spring is best for repairs before monsoon, and fall works well for larger projects.
Is it safe to walk on my tile roof?
We do not recommend it. Concrete and clay tiles crack easily under foot if you step in the wrong place, and a broken tile exposes the underlayment. Falls are also a serious risk.
Do roofs need maintenance during Arizona summers?
Yes, mostly by watching for storm damage and keeping debris cleared during monsoon season. Avoid unnecessary foot traffic on the roof in midday heat, when materials are most easily damaged.
What can I check in my attic?
With a flashlight, look for water stains on the roof deck and rafters, damp or matted insulation, daylight coming through, and musty smells. Stay on the framing and avoid stepping between joists.
How often should flat or foam roofs be checked?
At least once a year and after major storms. Flat roofs depend on clear drains and an intact coating, so a pro should check for ponding, blisters and worn coating before monsoon season.
Should I keep records of roof maintenance?
Yes. Keep inspection reports, repair invoices, warranty paperwork and dated photos together. They help with warranty claims, insurance claims and questions from buyers when you sell.
When should I clean my gutters in Arizona?
Clean them in spring before monsoon season, again after storms that load them with debris, and in late fall before winter rains. Homes with nearby trees may need more frequent cleaning.

guides.title: How to Read and Compare Roofing Estimates | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: How to read and compare roofing estimates: scope, tear-off, underlayment, decking allowances, flashing, ventilation, permits, warranty and payment terms.
guides.h1: How to read and compare roofing estimates
guides.lead: Two roofing bids can be thousands of dollars apart and still both be honest, because they often describe different jobs. Here is how to read each line and compare them fairly.
guides.answer: To compare roofing estimates, line them up item by item: scope and roof area, tear-off, underlayment brand and type, decking replacement allowance, flashing, ventilation, permits, cleanup, warranty wording and payment schedule. The lowest total is only a good deal if it includes the same work, because missing items often come back as change orders.

sections.h2: Start with the basics on the page
sections.body:
Before you look at numbers, check the top of the estimate. It should show the contractor's legal business name, address, phone number and Arizona ROC license number, plus your name, the property address and the date. Make sure the business name matches the license you looked up at roc.az.gov.

The estimate should also say how long the price is good for. Material costs change, and an estimate from months ago may need to be updated before you sign.

sections.h2: Scope of work and roof area
sections.body:
The scope is the plain-language description of what will be done. Is this a repair, a re-felt that reuses existing tile, a full tear-off and replacement, a recoat, or a roof over an existing layer? Which slopes or sections are included? A patio cover or garage can be left out without you noticing.

Roofs are usually measured in squares, where one square is 100 square feet. If two estimates list very different areas for the same house, ask how each one measured. A difference in the measurement can explain a lot of the price difference.

For a replacement, the estimate should say whether the existing roof is being removed down to the deck, how many layers are coming off, and that disposal is included. Tear-off is labor intensive and the dumpster or haul-off is a real cost, so a bid that skips it is not comparable to one that includes it.

For tile roofs, check whether the plan is to reuse the existing tile in a lift-and-relay or to replace it. Our tile underlayment guide explains the difference.

On Arizona roofs, especially tile, the underlayment does the waterproofing, so this line matters. A vague entry like underlayment or felt is not enough. Look for the type and weight, such as 30# felt, a two-layer system or a named synthetic product, and how many layers. If one bid uses a single layer of felt and another uses a high-temperature synthetic, they are not the same roof, even if the tile on top is identical.

Nobody can see the full condition of the roof deck until the old roof is off. Good estimates handle this honestly with a decking allowance or unit price, for example a price per sheet of plywood or OSB replaced, and sometimes a number of sheets included in the base price.

Compare the unit prices across bids, not just the totals. A low base price paired with a high per-sheet charge can cost more in the end. Ask the contractor to show you or photograph damaged decking before replacing it.

Many leaks start at flashings rather than in the field of the roof. Look for line items covering valley flashing, wall and step flashing, drip edge, vent pipe flashings, chimney or skylight flashing, and whether existing metal flashing is being replaced or reused. Reusing sound flashing can be fine, but the estimate should say which.

Ventilation affects attic heat, energy use and how long the roof lasts in Arizona. The estimate should note what vents are being installed or replaced, such as ridge vents, off-ridge vents or eyebrow vents on tile, and whether the plan meets code for your attic.
bullets: Valley, wall and step flashing: replaced, reset or reused?
Drip edge and eave details.
Pipe and vent flashings, and roof jacks.
Skylight, chimney and equipment curbs.
Attic ventilation type and number of vents.

sections.body: A complete estimate says who pulls the permit and whether permit fees are included. It should also describe cleanup, including haul-off of debris and a magnetic sweep for nails in the yard, driveway and pool area. Ask how they protect landscaping, AC units and pools during tear-off.

There are usually two kinds of warranty on a roof. The manufacturer's warranty covers defects in materials, and its terms depend on the product and sometimes on registration. The contractor's workmanship warranty covers installation. They are not the same, and one does not replace the other.

Read the actual words, not just a number of years. What exactly is covered? Is labor included or only materials? Is it transferable if you sell? What voids it, such as other trades walking on the roof or adding solar? A warranty is only as good as the company standing behind it, so ask how long the contractor has been in business and how warranty calls are handled. Get the warranty in writing as part of the contract.

The estimate or contract should spell out when payments are due: any deposit, progress payments and the final payment. Payments should follow progress, with the final payment due after the work is complete and inspected. Be cautious of a schedule that asks for most of the money before work starts. Ask about financing options during the estimate if you need them.

sections.h2: Why the cheapest bid isn't always cheapest
sections.body:
A low bid can be low for good reasons, such as lower overhead or a simpler approach. It can also be low because it leaves out tear-off, uses a lighter underlayment, reuses worn flashing, has a small decking allowance with a steep unit price, or skips permits. Those gaps often come back later as change orders or as a roof that leaks sooner.

The best way to compare is to make a simple side-by-side list of every item above and fill it in for each bid. Wherever a line is blank, ask. For a general sense of what drives roofing costs, see our Roofing Cost Guide, and remember every roof is different. To get an estimate from us, call 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: Why are my roofing estimates so different?

Estimates often differ because they describe different work, such as tear-off versus overlay, different underlayment, different flashing scope or different decking allowances. Compare each line item before comparing totals.
What is a roofing square?
A roofing square is 100 square feet of roof surface. Contractors use squares to measure the roof and price materials and labor, so check that each estimate lists a similar area.
What is a decking allowance?

It is a set amount or unit price in the estimate for replacing damaged roof deck found after the old roof is removed. Compare the per-sheet price across bids, and ask to see the damage before it is replaced.
Should the estimate name the underlayment brand?
Yes. The type, weight and number of layers, or the named synthetic product, should be in writing. It is one of the biggest differences in how long an Arizona roof lasts.
What is the difference between a manufacturer and workmanship warranty?

A manufacturer warranty covers defects in roofing materials, while a workmanship warranty from the contractor covers how the roof was installed. Read the written terms of each, including what is covered and what voids it.
Should permits be included in a roofing estimate?
A complete estimate should say who pulls the permit and whether permit fees are included. If it does not mention permits, ask before you sign.
Is it okay to ask a roofer to match another bid?
You can ask, but first make sure the bids include the same scope. Asking a contractor to match a lower price without matching the work can push them to cut items that matter.
Can I get financing for a roof?
Many contractors, including us, offer financing options. Ask about them during your estimate so you can compare the payment terms along with the scope.

guides.title: Roof Repair or Replacement in Arizona? | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Repair or replace your roof? Weigh Arizona roof age by type, damage, leak history, underlayment, energy, resale, HOA, solar and budget, plus a checklist.
guides.h1: Repair or replace your roof? An Arizona decision guide
guides.lead: Most roofs reach a point where you have to decide between another repair and a bigger project. These are the factors that matter most in Arizona and a simple checklist to help you decide.
guides.answer: Repair your roof when damage is limited, the materials and underlayment are in good shape, and leaks are isolated. Consider replacement, or a tile underlayment replacement, when the roof is near the end of its expected life, leaks keep returning, damage is widespread, or you plan to add solar or sell soon.

sections.body:
A repair fixes a specific problem. A replacement renews the whole system. The right choice depends on how much life the roof has left, not just how bad the current problem looks. A single cracked tile on a healthy roof is a repair. Repeated leaks on a roof with brittle underlayment are a sign that repairs are just buying time.

On Arizona tile roofs there is often a middle option: a lift-and-relay, or re-felt, that replaces the underlayment and reuses the tile. It is worth asking about before you choose between a small repair and a full replacement.

sections.h2: Roof age by type in Arizona
sections.body: Age is a starting point, not a verdict. Arizona's heat and UV shorten the life of some materials, while others hold up well. Installation quality, ventilation, roof pitch and maintenance all shift the numbers. In general terms:
bullets: Concrete and clay tile: the tile itself can last for decades, but the underlayment under it usually wears out much sooner and becomes the limiting factor.
Asphalt shingles: heat and sun break down shingles faster than in milder climates, so watch for curling, cracking and granule loss as they age.
Spray foam roofs: the foam can last a long time if the protective coating is maintained and recoated on schedule.
Elastomeric and other coatings on flat roofs: these need periodic recoating, and their life depends heavily on the coating and how well the roof drains.
Built-up and other flat roof systems: ponding water and UV are the main enemies, so drainage condition matters as much as age.

sections.body:
How much of the roof is affected matters more than how dramatic the damage looks. A few broken tiles or a lifted section of shingles after a monsoon storm is usually a straightforward repair. Damage spread across several slopes, widespread hail bruising or many slipped tiles suggests the roof as a whole has been weakened.

Ask your roofer to estimate what share of the roof is damaged and to show you photos. If repairs would touch a large part of the roof, a replacement may make more sense and may give you a more uniform result.

One leak that was fixed and never came back is a good sign. Leaks that return in the same area, or show up in new areas every monsoon season, usually mean the problem is not a single bad spot but a system that is failing. Each leak also risks damage to decking, insulation, drywall and framing that adds up over time.

Keep a record of when and where leaks happen. That history helps a roofer see the pattern and recommend the right fix.

On tile roofs, underlayment condition often decides the question. If a roofer lifts a few tiles and finds brittle, cracked or torn felt, spot repairs will keep chasing leaks. Replacing the underlayment, either in a lift-and-relay or as part of a full replacement, addresses the cause. Our tile roof underlayment guide covers the signs and the process.

Energy. A roof replacement is a chance to improve attic ventilation and, on flat roofs, add a reflective coating or foam that can reduce heat gain. In Arizona, where cooling is a big part of household energy use, that can matter. Results depend on the house, so treat energy savings as a benefit to discuss rather than a guarantee.

Resale. Buyers and their inspectors look closely at roofs. An old roof or a history of leaks can come up in negotiations, while a recent permitted replacement with warranty paperwork is easier to explain. If you plan to sell in the next few years, factor that in.

HOA. Many Valley HOAs control roof color and material. A repair that uses matching tile is usually simple. A full replacement or a change of material may need HOA approval, which can add time, so check the rules early.

If you plan to add solar panels, think about the roof first. Panels sit on the roof for many years, and removing and reinstalling them later to replace a roof adds cost and hassle. If your roof or underlayment is near the end of its life, it often makes sense to do the roof work before the panels go on. Talk with both your roofer and your solar installer about timing and how penetrations will be sealed.

Repairs cost less now, but a string of repairs on a failing roof can add up and still end in replacement. A replacement costs more up front but resets the clock. Some homeowners plan ahead by budgeting for a replacement or re-felt within a few years while handling small repairs in the meantime.

Every roof is different, so see our Roofing Cost Guide for what affects cost, and get a written estimate. Financing is available, and you can ask about it during the estimate. Our guide to reading a roofing estimate helps you compare options.
Answer each question honestly. The more times you answer yes, the more a replacement or underlayment replacement makes sense over another repair.
bullets: Is the roof, or the underlayment under the tile, near or past its expected life?
Have you had leaks in more than one place, or the same leak more than once?
Does damage cover more than a small, isolated area?
Did a roofer find brittle or torn underlayment, soft decking or widespread worn flashing?
Are you planning to install solar panels in the next few years?
Are you planning to sell the home soon?
Would repairs touch a large part of the roof anyway?
Are energy use and attic heat a concern you want to address?

sections.body: We have been repairing and replacing roofs in the Valley since 1993, and we will tell you when a repair is enough. Learn about our repairs and maintenance and roof replacement services, or call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: How do I know if my roof needs to be replaced?

Common signs include repeated leaks, widespread damage, brittle underlayment on a tile roof, and a roof near the end of its expected life. A professional inspection with photos is the most reliable way to decide.
Can a tile roof be repaired instead of replaced?
Often yes. Broken tiles and flashing can be repaired, and if the underlayment is worn, a lift-and-relay can replace it while reusing the existing tile.
Is it worth repairing an old roof?
It can be, if the damage is limited and the rest of the roof is sound. If the roof is near the end of its life and leaks keep returning, repair money may be better spent toward replacement.
Should I replace my roof before installing solar?
If the roof or underlayment has limited life left, it usually makes sense to do the roof work first. Removing and reinstalling panels later adds cost and complexity.
Does a new roof help when selling a house?
A recent, permitted roof with warranty paperwork can make inspections and negotiations smoother. An old or leaking roof is often a point buyers raise.
Do I need HOA approval to replace my roof?
Many Arizona HOAs require approval for roof replacement, especially if the color or material changes. Check your HOA rules before scheduling the work.
Can a new roof lower my energy bills?
Better attic ventilation and reflective coatings can reduce heat gain, which may help with cooling in Arizona. Results depend on the house, so treat it as a possible benefit rather than a promise.
Is financing available for roof replacement?
Yes, we offer financing. Ask about it during your estimate so you can compare repair and replacement options with payments in mind.

guides.title: Storm Damage and Roof Insurance Claims in AZ | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: What to do after a monsoon damages your Arizona roof: document safely, call your insurer, prepare for the adjuster, protect the home and avoid storm chasers.
guides.h1: Storm damage and roof insurance claims in Arizona
guides.lead: A monsoon can lift tiles, tear shingles and drive rain under a roof in minutes. This guide walks through what to do in the hours and weeks after a storm, from safe photos to the adjuster visit.
guides.answer: After storm damage, stay off the roof, photograph what you can see from the ground and inside, and limit further water damage with buckets and tarps on belongings. Call your insurance company to report the loss and ask how they handle roof claims, then have a licensed Arizona roofer inspect and document the damage. This guide is general information, not legal or insurance advice; your policy and your insurer decide what is covered.

sections.h2: First, a note on what this guide is
sections.body:
Every insurance policy is different, and only your insurer can tell you what your policy covers, what your deductible is and how their claim process works. This guide shares general guidance we have learned from years of repairing storm-damaged roofs in the Valley. It is not legal or insurance advice.

If you have questions about your rights as a policyholder, the Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions has consumer resources, and a licensed insurance agent or attorney can answer questions about your specific situation.

sections.h2: Stay safe right after the storm
sections.body:
Monsoon season in Arizona runs June 15–September 30, and the worst storms often bring high wind, dust, lightning and sudden heavy rain. Wait until the storm has fully passed before you go outside. Watch for downed power lines, broken branches hanging in trees and loose tiles or debris that could still fall from the roof edge.

Do not climb onto the roof. Wet tile, loose granules and storm debris make roofs slick, and a damaged deck may not hold your weight. A fall from a single-story roof can cause serious injury. Everything you need to document can be done from the ground and from inside the house.

sections.h2: Document the damage from the ground and inside
sections.body: Good records make the rest of the process easier. Start as soon as it is safe and keep everything in one folder on your phone or computer.
bullets: Take wide photos of each side of the house, then closer shots of any damage you can see from the yard.
Photograph tiles, shingle pieces or flashing that landed in the yard before you move them, then set them aside.
Use binoculars or your phone's zoom to capture missing tiles, lifted shingles, bent drip edge or torn coating.
Inside, photograph ceiling stains, drips, wet insulation in the attic and any damaged belongings.
Write down the date and approximate time of the storm and anything you noticed, such as a loud bang or when the leak started.
Keep receipts for buckets, tarps, fans, a hotel stay or anything else you buy because of the damage.

sections.h2: Prevent more damage while you wait
sections.body:
Most homeowner policies expect you to take reasonable steps to keep damage from getting worse. Inside the house, that can mean moving furniture and electronics, catching drips in buckets, laying towels down and running fans. If a ceiling is bulging with water, keep people away from it and call a professional; do not poke it while standing under it.

On the roof itself, temporary protection such as a tarp is best done by a roofer. Tarping a tile roof is tricky because walking on tile breaks it and a tarp that is weighted or nailed the wrong way can cause new leaks. Call us at 602-548-3770 to schedule an inspection. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

Report the loss to your insurer as soon as you reasonably can. Many policies have time limits for reporting damage, so do not wait weeks to see if the leak goes away. When you call, have your policy number, the date of the storm and your photos ready.

Ask questions and write down the answers, along with the name of each person you speak with:
bullets: Is the claim number assigned, and who is my adjuster?
What is my deductible for wind or storm damage?
Will an adjuster inspect the roof in person, and how soon?
Do you want a roofer's inspection report or repair estimate before the adjuster visit?
Are temporary repairs covered, and what documentation do you need for them?

sections.h2: What to expect at the adjuster visit
sections.body:
The adjuster works for the insurance company and is there to look at the damage and decide what the policy covers. Many adjusters will walk the roof, measure it and photograph damaged areas. Some homeowners like to have their roofer present so both people are looking at the same tiles, shingles and flashing at the same time.

Share your photos, your timeline and your roofer's report. Afterward, the insurer will usually send a written estimate or a letter explaining their decision. Read it closely. If something seems missing, such as underlayment damage the adjuster did not see, ask your insurer how to request a review and provide any supporting documentation.

sections.h2: What a roofer's inspection report should include
sections.body: A clear inspection report gives you and your insurer a shared record of the roof's condition. When we inspect a storm-damaged roof, we look at the whole system, not just the obvious broken pieces. A useful report typically covers:
bullets: The roof type, approximate age if known, and overall condition before the storm, where it can be judged.
Labeled photos of each area of damage, with notes on where it is on the roof.
Broken, slipped or missing tile; creased, torn or missing shingles; lifted or damaged flashing; damaged coating on flat roofs.
Signs of water getting past the top layer, such as wet or torn underlayment and stained decking.
Interior and attic observations that line up with the roof damage.
Recommended repairs or replacement, and what can wait versus what needs attention now.

sections.h2: How to spot and avoid storm chasers
sections.body: After a big monsoon, crews sometimes arrive from out of town, knock on doors and push homeowners to sign on the spot. Some do poor work and leave before problems show up. Take your time, even when water is coming in.
bullets: Look up any contractor's license on the Arizona Registrar of Contractors website before you sign anything.
Be wary of anyone who asks you to sign a contract or an assignment of your insurance benefits at the door.
Be cautious if someone offers to waive or cover your deductible; that is a red flag, and your deductible is part of your agreement with your insurer.
Ask for a local office address and phone number, and confirm they are real.
Avoid paying a large amount up front in cash.
Get the scope of work, materials and timeline in writing.

sections.body:
Some storm damage is a straightforward repair, such as replacing a handful of broken tiles. Other times the wind has damaged the underlayment across a large area, or an older roof cannot be repaired cleanly, and replacement makes more sense. A good roofer will explain the difference and show you why.

Every roof is different, so we do not quote prices without seeing it. For a general sense of what affects cost, read our Roofing Cost Guide, and see our storm damage repair and roof inspection pages for more on how we help.

faqs: Does homeowners insurance cover monsoon roof damage in Arizona?

Many policies cover sudden damage from wind, hail or falling objects, but coverage depends on your specific policy. Wear and tear, old age and long-term leaks are often excluded. Call your insurer and ask them to explain your coverage and deductible for storm damage.
Should I call my roofer or my insurance company first?

You can do both on the same day. Reporting the loss promptly to your insurer starts the claim, and a roofer's inspection gives you a clear picture of the damage. Ask your insurer whether they want a roofer's report before or after the adjuster visit.
Can I put a tarp on my roof myself?

We do not recommend it, especially on tile. Walking on tile breaks it, and ladders and wet surfaces after a storm are dangerous. Focus on protecting the inside of your home and have a roofer handle temporary protection on the roof.
How do I know if a roofer is licensed in Arizona?

Search the contractor's name or license number on the Arizona Registrar of Contractors website. The listing shows whether the license is active and the type of work it covers. Integrity Roofing's license is ROC #096629.
What if the adjuster misses some of the damage?

Read the insurer's estimate carefully and compare it with your photos and your roofer's report. If something looks missing, contact your insurer, ask how they handle a review or supplement, and send any supporting documentation they request.
How long do I have to file a roof damage claim?

Time limits vary by policy and insurer, so check your policy or ask your agent. In general, report damage as soon as you reasonably can. Waiting can make it harder to show the damage came from a specific storm.
Is a leak after a storm always storm damage?

Not always. A storm can expose an older problem, such as underlayment that was already worn out under the tile. A careful inspection helps separate new storm damage from long-term wear, which matters because insurers often treat them differently.
Do you work directly with insurance companies?

We inspect the roof, document the damage with photos and notes, and can share that report with you to provide to your insurer. Decisions about coverage are made by your insurance company. Call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm, to schedule an inspection.

guides.title: Solar Panels and Your Arizona Roof | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Thinking about solar in Arizona? Learn how roof age, mounting, flashing and detach-and-reset work affect your roof, and who to call if a solar roof leaks.
guides.h1: Solar panels and your roof: what Arizona homeowners should know
guides.lead: Solar panels can sit on your roof for decades, so the roof under them matters. Here is how to plan solar around your roof's age, type and condition, and how to avoid leaks later.
guides.answer: Before you install solar, have your roof inspected and make sure it has enough life left to outlast the panels, because removing and reinstalling a system later adds cost and hassle. On tile roofs the underlayment is the main concern, since it often wears out before the tile. Every bolt that goes through the roof needs proper flashing, and you should know in writing who is responsible if a mount leaks.

sections.h2: Check the roof's age and condition before you go solar
sections.body:
Solar panels are designed to last a long time. If your roof needs major work a few years after the panels go up, the system has to come off so the roof can be repaired or replaced, then go back on. Planning ahead avoids paying for that twice.

Ask a roofer to inspect the roof before you sign a solar contract. On an asphalt shingle roof, look at shingle age, granule loss and curling. On a concrete or clay tile roof, the tile itself can last a very long time, but the underlayment beneath it is what keeps water out, and in Arizona heat it often wears out well before the tile does. If the underlayment is near the end of its life, replacing it before solar goes on is usually the smarter order.

Detach and reset is the process of removing solar panels and racking, setting them aside safely, doing the roof work, and then reinstalling the system. It comes up when you re-roof, replace tile underlayment, or repair a leak under the array.

The electrical side of a solar system should be handled by a licensed solar or electrical contractor. In most cases your solar company, or a company that specializes in this work, removes and reinstalls the panels while the roofer handles the roof. We coordinate timing with your solar company so the roof is ready when they return. Ask both companies for a clear schedule, and ask the solar company whether reinstalling affects any warranty on the system.

sections.h2: Penetrations and flashing: where leaks start
sections.body: Most solar systems on sloped roofs are held down by mounts bolted through the roof into the rafters. Each of those bolts is a hole in your roof. Done well, every mount is flashed so water sheds around it. Done poorly, a mount sealed only with caulk or sealant can start leaking once the sealant dries out and cracks in the sun.
bullets: Each mount should be anchored into structure, not just the roof deck.
Mounts should have proper flashing that laps correctly with the roofing material above and below it.
Sealant can help, but it should not be the only thing keeping water out.
Wire runs and conduit that pass through the roof need their own properly flashed penetrations.
Ask your installer what mounting system they use and how they flash it on your roof type.

sections.body:
Tile roofs are common across the East Valley, and they take more care with solar. Concrete and clay tile cracks if it is stepped on the wrong way, and installers have to walk the roof to place mounts. Broken tiles under the array can go unnoticed for years.

There are a few common approaches. Tile hooks attach to the rafters and reach out between tiles so the tile can be put back. Another method removes tile at each mount location and replaces it with a flashed base. Either way, the underlayment under the tile must be protected and sealed at every penetration. After installation, it is worth having the roof checked for cracked or slipped tiles. See our tile roofs page for more on how tile roofs are built.

sections.h2: Solar on flat and foam roofs
sections.body:
Many Arizona homes, especially older ones and those with Pueblo or territorial styles, have flat or low-slope roofs. Solar on these roofs may use a tilted racking system that is either weighted down with ballast or attached through the roof.

On a spray foam roof, each attachment needs to be sealed into the foam and coating system so water cannot get into the foam. Racking should also leave room to recoat the roof, because foam roofs need periodic recoating. Heavy ballast and foot paths need to be planned so they do not crush or wear the roof surface. If your flat roof is due for a recoat or repair, do it before the panels go on.

sections.h2: Who is responsible if a solar roof leaks?
sections.body: This is one of the most common questions we hear, and the answer depends on your contracts. In general, the company that made the penetration is responsible for the leaks at that penetration, and the roofer is responsible for the roofing work they did. Warranties vary a lot, so read them before you sign.
bullets: Ask the solar company in writing whether they warrant roof penetrations and for how long.
Ask whether using a different roofer later, for repairs or detach and reset, affects that warranty.
Keep copies of your solar contract, roof warranty and any inspection photos together.
If a leak shows up under the panels, call the solar installer and a roofer so the cause can be traced.
If your solar company is no longer in business, a roofer can still find and repair the leak.

sections.h2: Critter guards keep birds and debris out
sections.body:
The gap between panels and the roof is a shaded, sheltered spot, and pigeons love it. Nesting birds leave droppings, nesting material and debris that hold moisture, clog roof valleys and can damage wiring. Critter guard is a mesh barrier installed around the edges of the array to keep animals out.

If you already have birds under your panels, the nesting material should be cleaned out before guards are installed. The mesh should attach to the panel frames, not be screwed into the roof, so it does not add new holes.

The best results come when the roof and the solar system are planned as a pair. Get the roof inspected, handle any repairs or replacement first, and share your roof's details with the solar installer. If you are not sure whether your roof is ready, call us at 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. For a general sense of re-roofing costs, see our Roofing Cost Guide.

faqs: Should I replace my roof before installing solar?

If your roof is close to the end of its life, it usually makes sense to replace it, or replace tile underlayment, before solar goes on. That avoids paying to remove and reinstall the panels a few years later. An inspection will tell you how much life the roof has left.
Can solar panels be installed on a tile roof?

Yes. Installers commonly use tile hooks or replace tile at each mount with a flashed base. The key is protecting and sealing the underlayment at every penetration and replacing any tile that cracks during installation.
Do solar panels cause roof leaks?

Panels themselves do not, but the mounts and wire penetrations can if they are not flashed and sealed correctly. Most solar-related leaks we see trace back to a mount, a conduit penetration or tiles broken during installation.
Who removes my solar panels when I re-roof?

Usually your solar company or a company that specializes in detach and reset handles the panels and electrical work. The roofer does the roof work in between. We coordinate the schedule with your solar company.
Do solar panels protect my roof from the sun?

Panels do shade the part of the roof they cover, which can reduce heat and UV exposure there. The roof around the array still ages normally, and the area under the panels is harder to inspect, so it still needs attention.
How do I keep pigeons out from under my solar panels?
Have the area cleaned out and then install critter guard mesh around the array. The mesh should clip to the panel frames rather than being screwed into the roof, so it does not create new holes.
Can solar go on a foam roof?

Yes, but each attachment must be sealed into the foam and coating so water cannot get in. Plan the layout so the roof can still be recoated, and handle any needed recoat or repairs before the panels are installed.
Does Integrity Roofing install solar panels?

No. We are roofers, not solar installers. We inspect roofs before solar, repair and replace roofs under existing systems, and coordinate with your solar company when panels need to come off and go back on.

guides.title: Attic Heat and Roof Ventilation in Arizona | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: How attic ventilation, cool roofs, radiant barriers and insulation work in Arizona heat, how heat ages your roof, and the signs your attic is poorly vented.
guides.h1: Attic heat, roof ventilation and energy in Arizona
guides.lead: In a Phoenix-area summer, the attic is often the hottest place in the house. How your roof breathes affects your cooling bills, your comfort and how long your roof lasts.
guides.answer: A well-vented attic pulls cooler air in low at the eaves or soffits and lets hot air out high near the ridge, keeping that intake and exhaust balanced. In Arizona, good ventilation, proper insulation and a reflective roof surface work together to reduce attic heat. Less heat in the attic helps underlayment and shingles last longer and makes your air conditioner's job easier.

sections.h2: Why attic heat matters so much in Arizona
sections.body:
Arizona sun beats down on roofs for most of the year. On a summer afternoon, a dark roof surface gets far hotter than the air temperature, and that heat soaks through into the attic. In an attic with poor airflow, the heat builds hour after hour and does not fully clear out overnight.

That trapped heat pushes down through the ceiling into your living space and heats any air ducts running through the attic. It also bakes the roofing materials from below while the sun bakes them from above.

sections.h2: Intake and exhaust: how ventilation works
sections.body: Attic ventilation relies on a simple idea: hot air rises. A balanced system has two parts.
bullets: Intake vents sit low on the roof, usually in the soffits or at the eaves, and let cooler outside air in.
Exhaust vents sit high, near the ridge, and let hot air escape. Common types include ridge vents, low-profile off-ridge vents, turbine vents and gable vents.
Air should flow from the intake, across the underside of the roof deck, and out the exhaust.
Intake and exhaust should be roughly balanced. Too much exhaust and not enough intake can pull air from the wrong places, including from inside your house.
Mixing different exhaust types on the same roof can short-circuit airflow, with one vent pulling air in through another instead of from the eaves.

sections.h2: How much ventilation does a roof need?
sections.body:
Building codes set a minimum amount of net free vent area based on the size of the attic floor. A common rule of thumb is 1 square foot of ventilation for every 150 square feet of attic floor, or 1 for every 300 when the system is balanced between high and low vents and meets certain conditions. Your local code and the vent manufacturer's ratings decide the exact numbers.

When we replace a roof, we look at the existing ventilation and recommend changes if it is not enough or not balanced. Vents also have to work with the roof type; tile roofs use vents designed to sit with the tile profile, and shingle roofs commonly use ridge vents or off-ridge vents.

sections.h2: How heat ages underlayment and shingles
sections.body:
Heat and UV are the main reasons roofs wear out in Arizona. On asphalt shingle roofs, years of high heat dry out the asphalt, which can lead to curling, cracking, blistering and faster granule loss. A hot attic adds heat from underneath, which can shorten shingle life further.

On tile roofs, the tile is durable, but the underlayment beneath it is what actually keeps water out. Traditional felt underlayment gets brittle as it bakes year after year and eventually cracks, especially at the eaves, valleys and around penetrations. That is why tile roofs in the Valley often need the underlayment replaced, a job called a re-felt or lift and relay, long before the tile itself is worn out.

A cool roof is designed to reflect more sunlight and release absorbed heat more easily than a standard roof. Lighter colors and specially rated materials stay noticeably cooler in direct sun. The Cool Roof Rating Council publishes independent ratings for solar reflectance and thermal emittance that let you compare products.

On flat roofs, a white elastomeric coating or a coated spray foam roof is one of the most effective ways to reduce heat. On sloped roofs, lighter tile or shingle colors help, though color choices may be limited by your HOA. Keep in mind that coatings get dirty and wear over time, and a dirty or worn coating reflects less.

A radiant barrier is a reflective material, often foil-faced sheathing or a foil sheet stapled to the underside of the rafters, that reduces the amount of heat radiating from the hot roof deck down into the attic. Radiant barriers tend to work best in hot, sunny climates like ours, and the U.S. Department of Energy notes they can be especially helpful when ducts run through the attic.

For a radiant barrier to work, the shiny side needs an air space facing it, and it should not be laid directly on top of attic insulation where dust will collect and reduce its effect. It does not replace ventilation or insulation; it works alongside them.

Ventilation moves heat out of the attic. Insulation slows heat from moving through the ceiling into your home. You need both. Insulation is rated by R-value; the higher the number, the more it resists heat flow. The Department of Energy's Energy Saver site lists recommended attic R-values by climate zone, and it is a good place to check what fits the Phoenix area.
bullets: Insulation should be spread evenly, without bare spots or thin areas near the eaves.
Insulation should not block soffit vents. Baffles keep a clear air channel at the eaves.
Compressed, wet or rodent-damaged insulation loses much of its value and should be replaced.
Sealing gaps around light fixtures, attic hatches and plumbing keeps conditioned air out of the attic.

sections.h2: Signs your attic is poorly ventilated
sections.body: Many ventilation problems are easy to spot once you know what to look for. Some signs show up inside the house, and some on the roof.
bullets: Upstairs rooms that stay much hotter than the rest of the house.
An attic that feels like an oven even in the early morning.
Soffit vents that are painted over, blocked by insulation or missing.
Shingles that are curling, blistering or losing granules faster than expected.
Brittle, cracked underlayment visible at the eaves of a tile roof.
Signs of condensation, such as rusty nail tips or stains on the underside of the roof deck, which can happen in winter or monsoon humidity.

sections.body: If your attic runs hot or your roof is aging faster than it should, a roof inspection can check vents, underlayment and roof surface together. Call us at 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. If a new roof is on the table, our Roofing Cost Guide explains what affects the price.

faqs: What is the difference between intake and exhaust vents?

Intake vents sit low, usually in the soffits or eaves, and let outside air into the attic. Exhaust vents sit high near the ridge and let hot air out. A good system has both, roughly balanced, so air moves steadily across the underside of the roof.
Can I have too much attic ventilation?

It is possible to have the wrong kind. Adding lots of exhaust without enough intake, or mixing exhaust types, can pull air from inside your home or from one vent into another. Balance matters more than simply adding more vents.
Does a lighter roof color really make a difference in Arizona?
Yes. Lighter, more reflective surfaces absorb less sun and stay cooler than dark ones, which can reduce attic heat. On sloped roofs, check your HOA's approved colors before choosing.
Are radiant barriers worth it in Phoenix?

Radiant barriers are most effective in hot, sunny climates and when ducts run through the attic, which describes many Valley homes. They work best alongside good ventilation and insulation, not as a substitute for either.
Should attic fans be used in Arizona?
