Powered attic fans can help in some homes, but they can also pull cooled air out of the house through ceiling gaps if the attic does not have enough intake. Have the whole system evaluated before adding one.
Why does my tile roof need new underlayment if the tiles look fine?

In Arizona heat, the underlayment under the tile often wears out long before the tile does. Once it cracks, water that gets past the tile can reach the deck. Replacing it while reusing good tile is called a re-felt or lift and relay.
Does a new roof fix ventilation problems?
It is the best time to fix them. During a replacement, vents can be added, removed or rebalanced to suit the roof and attic. We review ventilation as part of every replacement.
How can I tell if my attic insulation is enough?

Look for even coverage with no bare spots, and measure the depth in a few places. Compare it with the recommended R-values for our climate on the Department of Energy's Energy Saver site, or ask an insulation contractor to check.

guides.title: Caring for Flat and Foam Roofs in Arizona | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Keep your Arizona flat or spray foam roof healthy: manage ponding, clear drains and scuppers, check parapets, time recoats, and handle blisters and bird damage.
guides.h1: Caring for flat and foam roofs in Arizona
guides.lead: Flat and low-slope roofs are common across the Valley, from older ranch homes to Pueblo-style houses and commercial buildings. A little regular care keeps them watertight and helps them last.
guides.answer: Flat and foam roofs last longest when water drains off quickly, drains and scuppers stay clear, and the protective coating is renewed before it wears through. Check the roof after monsoon storms and at least once a year, watch for ponding, blisters, cracks and bird damage, and keep foot traffic to a minimum. Recoating a foam roof on time is far easier than repairing foam that has been exposed to the sun.

sections.h2: How flat and foam roofs are built
sections.body:
Flat roofs are not perfectly flat; they have a slight slope so water can drain toward drains, scuppers or gutters. Common flat roof systems in Arizona include built-up roofs, modified bitumen, single-ply membranes and spray polyurethane foam, often called SPF or foam.

A foam roof is sprayed on as a liquid that expands into a seamless, insulating layer, then covered with a protective coating. The foam provides insulation and the waterproof body of the roof, but it breaks down quickly in UV light. The coating is what protects it, which is why coating care is the heart of foam roof maintenance. See our flat roofing page for more on each system.

Ponding is water that stays on the roof after a storm instead of draining away. A common industry guideline treats water that remains 48 hours after rain as ponding. In Arizona sun, small puddles often evaporate quickly, but repeated ponding in the same spot can wear coatings faster, collect dirt and debris, and add weight.

Ponding usually points to a low spot, a clogged drain or a roof that has settled. Small areas can sometimes be built up with additional foam or other material during a repair or recoat. Larger or deeper ponding areas should be looked at by a roofer to find the cause.

Water leaves most flat roofs through roof drains, scuppers (openings through the parapet wall) or canales, the decorative channels common on Pueblo-style homes. When these clog, water backs up and finds other ways into the building.
bullets: Check drains and scuppers before monsoon season starts on June 15 and after major storms.
Remove leaves, dirt, tennis balls, nesting material and other debris.
Look for cracks or gaps where the scupper or drain meets the roof surface.
Make sure water exiting a scupper or canale is directed away from walls and the foundation.
Keep tree branches trimmed back so leaves do not collect on the roof.

sections.body:
Parapets are the short walls that extend above the roof line on many flat-roof homes. They hide equipment and give homes their classic Southwest look, but they are a common source of leaks. Water can get in through cracked stucco on top of the wall, through gaps where the wall meets the roof, or through damaged parapet caps.

When you inspect, look at the tops of parapets for cracks and at the inside corners where the roof turns up the wall. On foam roofs, the foam and coating usually run up the inside of the parapet, and that transition should be smooth and intact. Stucco repair on the outside of a parapet may need a stucco contractor, while the roof side is roofer territory.

Coatings on foam and other flat roofs slowly wear away from sun, heat, weather and dirt. As the coating thins, it reflects less heat and protects less. Eventually the foam underneath shows through, often with a tan or orange color, and once foam is exposed to UV it starts to break down.

How often a roof needs a recoat depends on the coating type, how thick it was applied and how the roof is used. Many foam roofs are recoated every several years, and your roofer can give you a timeline for your specific system. The key is to recoat while the foam is still healthy. A timely recoat with an elastomeric coating is far less work than tearing out damaged foam.
bullets: Chalky residue that rubs off on your hand is normal aging, but heavy chalking means the coating is thinning.
Cracking or peeling coating should be repaired before water gets underneath.
Any exposed foam should be covered as soon as practical.
Annual checks make it easier to plan a recoat before damage starts.

sections.body:
Blisters are raised, bubble-like areas in a roof surface. On foam roofs, blisters can form when moisture gets trapped or when the foam or coating loses its bond. On built-up and other membrane roofs, trapped air or moisture between layers can cause similar bubbles.

Small, stable blisters are not always an emergency, but they should not be ignored. If a blister cracks or is punctured, water can get in. A roofer can cut out the damaged area, let it dry if needed, and fill and recoat it. Do not cut blisters open yourself.

Birds sometimes peck at foam roofs, leaving small holes or gouges. The soft foam under the coating is easy for them to dig into. Each hole is a place where water and UV can reach the foam.

Look for small pockmarks, especially near parapets, AC units and other spots where birds perch. Small holes can be filled and coated during routine maintenance. Hail and wind-blown debris during monsoon storms can also leave dents and punctures that should be sealed.

sections.h2: Foot traffic and rooftop HVAC units
sections.body: Many Arizona flat roofs carry air conditioning units, evaporative coolers, solar panels and vents. Each one brings service visits, and service visits bring foot traffic. Repeated walking wears through coatings, and dropped tools or screws can puncture the surface.
bullets: Ask HVAC technicians to stay on established paths and avoid dragging equipment.
Walk pads can protect high-traffic routes to equipment.
Check around HVAC units after service for screws, panels or debris left behind.
Look at the curbs and stands that support equipment, and at the seals around ductwork and electrical lines.
Evaporative coolers can drip or overflow; a leaking cooler can damage the roof over time.

sections.body: Call for help if you see exposed foam, standing water that does not drain, cracked coating, blisters, stains on ceilings below a flat roof, or damage after a storm. We handle repairs and maintenance, recoats and replacements on flat and foam roofs. Call us at 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. For a general idea of what affects pricing, see our Roofing Cost Guide.

faqs: How often should a foam roof be recoated?

It depends on the coating type, its thickness and how the roof is used. Many foam roofs are recoated every several years. An inspection can tell you how much coating is left and when to plan the next recoat.
What does it mean if I can see orange or tan foam?
It usually means the protective coating has worn through and the foam is exposed. UV light breaks down exposed foam, so the area should be repaired and recoated as soon as practical.
Is a little standing water on my flat roof a problem?
Small puddles that dry within a day or two are common. Water that stays longer, or ponds in the same spot after every storm, can wear the roof faster and should be looked at to find the cause.
Can a foam roof be repaired, or does it need to be replaced?

Many foam roofs can be repaired and recoated as long as the foam is mostly dry and in good shape. If large areas are wet or badly damaged, those areas or the whole roof may need to be removed and replaced.
Why are there small holes in my foam roof?

Birds pecking at the foam are a common cause, especially near parapets and rooftop equipment. Hail and debris can also cause punctures. Small holes can be filled and coated during routine maintenance.
How do I keep HVAC technicians from damaging my roof?
Ask them to use a set path, avoid dragging equipment and remove all screws and debris when they finish. Walk pads along common routes help protect the coating.
Should I clean my flat roof drains myself?

If you can safely reach the roof with a secure ladder and the roof is cool and dry, clearing loose debris from drains and scuppers is reasonable. If access is difficult or you are unsure, have a professional handle it.
Do flat roofs leak more than sloped roofs?
Not necessarily. A well-maintained flat roof with good drainage can perform very well. Flat roofs do depend more on clear drains and a healthy coating or membrane, so regular checks matter.

guides.title: HOA Roof Approval Guide for the East Valley | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Re-roofing in an East Valley HOA? Learn how architectural review works, what to send, matching tile profile and color, typical timelines and permit basics.
guides.h1: HOA approval for a re-roof in the East Valley
guides.lead: Many neighborhoods in Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Queen Creek and San Tan Valley have homeowners associations with rules about how roofs look. Getting approval before work starts keeps your project on track.
guides.answer: Most HOAs require architectural review approval before you replace a roof or change its color, tile profile or material. You typically send the HOA's request with the product name, color, profile and a sample or photo, then wait for a written approval before work starts. Rules and timelines differ by community, so read your HOA's guidelines and check with your city about building permits.

sections.body:
Roofs are one of the most visible parts of a home, and HOAs use design guidelines to keep a consistent look across the neighborhood. Many communities in the East Valley were built with concrete tile roofs in a set of colors chosen by the builder, and the HOA's guidelines often aim to keep that look as homes are re-roofed.

Every HOA is different. Some have a short list of approved roof colors and materials, others allow anything that matches the home's style, and some require approval only when you change the look. Your HOA's CC&Rs and architectural guidelines are the place to start.
Before you pick a tile or shingle, get the current documents from your HOA or its management company. They are often available through the community's website or resident portal.
bullets: The CC&Rs, which set out the community's restrictions.
The architectural or design guidelines, which usually cover roof materials, colors and profiles.
The architectural review request document and any instructions for completing it.
Any approved color palette or list of pre-approved roofing products.
Meeting schedules for the architectural review committee, if it meets on set dates.

sections.body: Many HOAs require approval for any exterior change, including a full re-roof, even if you plan to use the same material and color. Others only require it if something visible changes. Common situations that usually need approval include:
bullets: Replacing the roof with a different tile color, blend or profile.
Switching from tile to shingles, or the other way around, where the guidelines allow it.
Changing gutter, fascia or trim colors as part of the project.
Adding new visible items, such as roof vents in a different color or solar panels.

sections.body:
Concrete tile comes in several profiles, which describe the shape of each tile. Common ones include flat, low-profile S and high-profile S (often called Spanish or mission style). Colors range from single solid tones to blends of several shades. Your HOA may require the same profile and a similar color to the original, or a choice from an approved palette.

Exact matches can be hard, especially on older homes. Tile colors fade over time, and some original colors are no longer made. If you are only replacing underlayment through a re-felt or lift and relay, most of the existing tile is reused, so the look rarely changes, though a few replacement tiles may be needed. If a full tile replacement is planned, ask your roofer to bring samples so you can compare them with your home and your neighbors' roofs. Learn more on our tile roofs page.

sections.h2: What to include in an architectural review request
sections.body: A complete request is the fastest way to get approval. Incomplete requests are often sent back, which restarts the clock. Most HOAs ask for some combination of the following:
bullets: Your name, address and lot number, and the HOA's request document, completed in full.
The roofing manufacturer, product line, color name and profile.
A product brochure, color sheet or photo of the tile or shingle, and sometimes a physical sample.
A photo of your home as it is now.
The contractor's name and Arizona ROC license number. Ours is ROC #096629.
Notes on any other visible changes, such as vents, gutters or fascia color.
Your planned start date, if the HOA asks for one.

sections.body:
Review times vary widely. Some HOAs approve standard requests within days, while others only review at monthly committee meetings. Many guidelines state a maximum review period, so check yours. Plan ahead and send your request well before you hope to start, especially if you want the work done before monsoon season begins on June 15.

Wait for written approval before work begins. Starting without approval can lead to fines or a requirement to change the roof, and that is an expensive mistake. Keep a copy of the approval letter with your roofing contract and warranty paperwork.

HOA approval and a building permit are two different things. The HOA controls appearance in the community. The city or town controls building safety and code compliance. Whether a re-roof needs a permit, and what the permit requires, depends on your city and the scope of work.

Requirements differ between Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Queen Creek and other cities, and can also vary based on whether the roof deck or structure is changed. Check your city's building department website or call them for current rules. On jobs that require a permit, the roofing contractor typically pulls it; ask your roofer to confirm.

sections.h2: How we help with HOA projects
sections.body: We work in HOA communities across the East Valley. We can provide product information, color names, sample tiles and our license details for your request, and we schedule work after you have approval. See our pages on roof replacement and roofing in Gilbert, and our Roofing Cost Guide for what affects price. To get started, call 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: Do I need HOA approval to replace my roof with the same tile?

Many HOAs still require approval for a full re-roof, even with the same material and color. Others only require it if something visible changes. Check your architectural guidelines or ask your management company.
Do I need HOA approval for a re-felt or lift and relay?

Often not, since the existing tile is put back and the look does not change, but some HOAs want to be notified of any roof work. If replacement tiles will be noticeably different, ask before work starts.
What if my original tile color is no longer made?

This is common on older homes. Your roofer can bring samples of current colors that come close, and you can include them in your request. Some HOAs have an approved palette that lists acceptable replacements.
How long does HOA roof approval take?
It depends on the HOA. Some respond within days, while others review requests only at scheduled committee meetings. Your guidelines may list a maximum review time, so plan ahead.
Can my HOA make me use a specific roofing contractor?
HOAs typically regulate how a roof looks, not who installs it, though some have requirements such as licensing and insurance. Read your CC&Rs and guidelines or ask your management company.
Is a building permit required for a re-roof?

It depends on your city and the scope of the work. Rules differ between Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler and other cities. Check with your city's building department, and ask your roofer whether they will pull any permit required.
What happens if I re-roof without HOA approval?
Your HOA may issue a violation, charge fines or require changes if the roof does not meet the guidelines. Waiting for written approval avoids that risk.
Can I switch from tile to shingles in an HOA?
Some HOAs allow it and many do not, depending on the community's design standards. Check the architectural guidelines first, and include product details in your request if it is allowed.

guides.title: Safe DIY Roof Checks for Arizona Homes | Integrity Roofing
guides.desc: Check your roof safely from the ground and attic: what to spot with binoculars and a flashlight, ceiling stain clues, what not to do, and when to call a pro.
guides.h1: Safe DIY roof checks from the ground and the attic
guides.lead: You can learn a lot about your roof without ever climbing onto it. These checks help you spot problems early and know when it is time to call a roofer.
guides.answer: Homeowners can safely check a roof from the ground with binoculars and from the attic with a flashlight, looking for missing or broken tile, lifted shingles, damaged flashing, daylight, water stains and wet insulation. Do not walk on a tile roof and avoid climbing onto any roof, especially in Arizona heat. If you find stains, leaks or damage, call a licensed roofer.

sections.body: Falls from ladders and roofs cause serious injuries every year. Roofing crews use training and safety equipment for a reason. On top of the fall risk, Arizona roofs add a few hazards of their own.
bullets: Tile breaks. Concrete and clay tile cracks when stepped on in the wrong spot, and a broken tile can lead to a leak.
Heat. Roof surfaces in summer can get hot enough to burn skin, and heat exhaustion can set in quickly.
Slick surfaces. Loose granules, dust, dew and monsoon rain make roofs slippery.
Hidden damage. A weak or rotted deck may not hold your weight.

sections.body:
Pick a dry, calm day. In summer, do outdoor checks early in the morning when the light is good and temperatures are lower. Twice a year is a good habit, once before monsoon season starts on June 15 and once in the fall, plus a quick look after any big storm.

Bring binoculars or a phone with a good zoom, a notepad and a flashlight for the attic. Take photos each time so you can compare from year to year and show a roofer exactly what you saw.

sections.h2: What to look for from the ground
sections.body: Walk all the way around the house and look at each roof slope. Step back far enough to see the upper areas, and check from across the street if you have a two-story home.
bullets: Missing, cracked or slipped tiles, especially along ridges, hips and edges.
Shingles that are missing, curling, creased or lifted, or patches of darker color where granules have worn away.
Granules collecting in gutters or at downspout outlets.
Bent, loose or missing flashing around chimneys, walls, vents and skylights.
Damaged or missing roof vents and pipe boots.
Sagging areas or a ridge line that is not straight.
Peeling fascia paint or stained soffits, which can signal water at the roof edge.
Birds, pigeons or debris under solar panels.

sections.h2: Check the attic with a flashlight
sections.body:
The attic shows you the underside of the roof, which is often where leaks show up first. In summer, Arizona attics can get dangerously hot, so go in the early morning or wait for a cooler month. Tell someone you are going up, and limit your time.

Step only on joists or a floored walkway. The drywall between joists will not hold you, and a misstep can put a foot through the ceiling. Watch for nails sticking through the roof deck overhead, and wear a mask, gloves and long sleeves around insulation.
bullets: Water stains, dark spots or streaks on the underside of the roof deck and rafters.
Wet, matted or discolored insulation.
Daylight coming through the deck, other than at designed vents.
Signs of pests, such as droppings or chewed insulation.
Soffit vents blocked by insulation.
Damp areas around plumbing vents, exhaust fans and chimneys.

sections.h2: What ceiling stains can tell you
sections.body:
A ceiling stain is often the first sign a roof is leaking, but it does not always sit directly under the problem. Water can travel along rafters, the underlayment or the top of drywall before it shows up. A stain near an exterior wall may point to flashing or an edge problem, while a stain near a bathroom may be plumbing or an exhaust fan instead of the roof.

Watch whether the stain grows after rain. A stain that only appears after storms usually means a roof leak. A stain that grows when it has not rained may be plumbing, an AC drain line or condensation. Take a photo and mark the edge of the stain with pencil so you can tell if it spreads.

If you have gutters or a flat roof with scuppers, clear drainage matters before monsoon season. If you use a ladder, set it on firm, level ground, extend it at least 3 feet above the edge you are working at and keep three points of contact. Have someone hold the ladder.

Never lean a ladder against a gutter that is loose, and do not step from the ladder onto a tile roof. If you cannot reach something safely from the ladder, leave it for a pro.

• Do not walk on tile roofs; even a careful step can crack tiles.
  • Do not go on any roof during or right after a storm, or in high heat.
  • Do not pressure wash a roof; it can strip shingle granules, damage coatings and force water under tile.
  • Do not seal over a leak with caulk or roofing cement from the top; this often traps water and hides the real source.
  • Do not cut open blisters on flat or foam roofs.
  • Do not work near overhead power lines or solar wiring.

Call a licensed roofer if you see active leaks, ceiling stains, wet insulation, missing or broken tile, damaged flashing, exposed foam on a flat roof or anything you are unsure about. A professional roof inspection covers areas you cannot see from the ground, including underlayment and flashing under the tile. For repairs, see repairs and maintenance.

Call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Every roof is different; our Roofing Cost Guide explains what affects the cost of repairs and replacement.

faqs: How often should I check my roof myself?
Twice a year is a good routine, once before monsoon season and once in the fall. Also take a quick look from the ground after any major storm.
Can I walk on my tile roof if I am careful?

We recommend you do not. Concrete and clay tile can crack even under careful steps, and a cracked tile can let water reach the underlayment. Roofers know where to step and still sometimes need to replace tile.
Is it safe to go in my attic in summer?
Arizona attics can get extremely hot in summer, which can lead to heat exhaustion quickly. Go early in the morning or wait for cooler months, limit your time and tell someone you are up there.
What does daylight in my attic mean?
Light at designed vents is normal. Light coming through the roof deck itself can mean a hole or gap that water could also get through, and it should be checked by a roofer.
How do I know if a ceiling stain is from the roof?

If it appears or grows after rain, a roof leak is likely. If it changes when it has not rained, plumbing, an AC drain line or condensation may be the cause. A roofer can trace the source from the attic and roof.
What do binoculars help me see?
Binoculars let you spot broken or slipped tile, lifted shingles, damaged flashing and worn vents from the safety of the ground. Taking photos through a phone zoom works too and gives you a record.
Should I use roof sealant to fix a small leak?

We do not recommend it. Sealant on top of the roof often traps water or sends it somewhere else, and it makes the real problem harder to find. It is better to have the source found and repaired properly.
What should I tell a roofer when I call?
Describe where the stain or damage is, when you first noticed it and whether it changes after rain. Photos from the ground and attic are very helpful.

glossary: Asphalt shingle
A common sloped-roof covering made of a fiberglass mat coated with asphalt and topped with mineral granules. Shingles are lighter than tile and are installed in overlapping rows.
Architectural shingle
A thicker, multi-layer asphalt shingle, also called a dimensional or laminated shingle. It gives a more textured look than a flat three-tab shingle.
Three-tab shingle
A flat, single-layer asphalt shingle with cutouts that make each strip look like three separate pieces. It is thinner and lighter than an architectural shingle.
Granules
The small, colored mineral chips on the surface of asphalt shingles. They protect the asphalt from UV light, so heavy granule loss is a sign of aging.
Concrete tile
A heavy, durable roofing tile made from cement, sand and water, very common on Arizona homes. The tile sheds most water and sun, while the underlayment beneath it is the true waterproof layer.
Clay tile
A roofing tile made from fired clay, known for its classic Spanish and Mediterranean look. Clay tile holds its color well but can be brittle underfoot.
Tile profile
The shape of a roof tile, such as flat, low-profile S or high-profile S. HOAs often require a replacement roof to keep the same profile.
S-tile
A curved roof tile with an S-shaped profile that creates the rolling look of a Spanish or mission style roof. It comes in low- and high-profile versions.
Underlayment
The water-resistant layer installed on the roof deck beneath tile or shingles. On a tile roof it does most of the waterproofing, and in Arizona heat it often wears out before the tile.
Felt
A traditional underlayment made of paper or fiberglass saturated with asphalt, often sold by weight such as 30-pound felt. Over years of heat it can become brittle and crack.
Synthetic underlayment
A lightweight underlayment made from woven or spun plastic materials. It is tear-resistant and generally handles heat and UV exposure better than traditional felt.
Self-adhered underlayment
A peel-and-stick underlayment with a sticky back that bonds to the deck and seals around nails. It is often used in valleys, at eaves and around penetrations.
Two-ply underlayment
Two overlapping layers of underlayment installed for extra protection, commonly used under tile on lower-slope roofs. Requirements depend on the roof slope and the tile manufacturer.
Battens
Strips of wood or other material fastened across the roof deck to hold tiles in place. Some tile roofs use battens, while others have tiles fastened directly to the deck.
Bird stop
A shaped piece, often called eave closure, installed at the bottom edge of a tile roof to fill the open space under curved tiles. It keeps birds and pests from nesting under the tile.
Eave riser
A strip installed along the eave of a tile roof that raises the first row of tile so it sits at the same angle as the rows above. It helps the tile lie flat and drain properly.
Drip edge
A strip of metal flashing installed along roof edges that directs water away from the fascia and into gutters. It also helps protect the edge of the roof deck.
Eave
The lower edge of a roof that overhangs the wall of the house. Water drains off the roof at the eaves.
Rake
The sloped edge of a roof at the end of a gable, running from the eave up to the ridge. Rake tiles or trim finish this edge.
Ridge
The highest horizontal line on a sloped roof where two roof planes meet. It is capped with ridge tiles or ridge cap shingles.
Hip
The sloped line where two roof planes meet on an outside corner, running from the ridge down to the eave. Hips are covered with hip tiles or cap shingles.
Valley
The inside angle where two roof slopes meet and carry water down. Valleys handle a lot of water, so they are a common place for leaks when flashing or underlayment fails.
Gable
The triangular wall section at the end of a pitched roof. A gable roof has two slopes that meet at a central ridge.
Hip roof
A roof with slopes on all four sides that meet at hips and a ridge. There are no vertical gable ends.
Fascia
The vertical board along the roof edge that the gutters are usually attached to. Peeling paint or rot on the fascia can be a sign of water at the roof edge.
Soffit
The underside of the roof overhang, between the fascia and the house wall. Soffits often contain intake vents for the attic.
Overhang
The part of the roof that extends past the exterior walls. It shades walls and windows and keeps water away from the house.
Flashing
Thin pieces of metal or other material installed where the roof meets walls, chimneys, vents, skylights and valleys. Flashing directs water away from joints that would otherwise leak.
Counter-flashing
A second piece of flashing set into or attached to a wall or chimney that laps over the base flashing. It covers the top edge of the base flashing so water cannot get behind it.
Step flashing
Individual L-shaped pieces of flashing woven in with each course of shingles where a roof meets a side wall. Each piece overlaps the one below to shed water.
Headwall flashing
Flashing installed where the top of a roof slope meets a vertical wall. It keeps water from running behind the roofing at that joint.
Pipe boot
A flashing collar that fits around a plumbing vent pipe where it passes through the roof. Rubber parts on pipe boots can crack in the sun over time.
Penetration
Any opening that passes through the roof, such as vents, pipes, skylights, conduit or solar mounts. Every penetration needs proper flashing to stay watertight.
Cricket
A small peaked structure built behind a chimney or other roof obstruction to divert water around it. It keeps water from pooling on the uphill side.
Saddle
Another name for a cricket, the small ridge built to divert water around a chimney or curb.
Scupper
An opening through a parapet wall that lets water drain off a flat roof. Scuppers must stay clear of debris to prevent backups.
Canale
A decorative drain spout or channel that carries water off a flat roof through a parapet, common on Pueblo-style homes in Arizona.
Roof drain
A drain set into the surface of a flat roof that carries water down through internal piping. It needs regular cleaning to prevent ponding.
Parapet
A low wall that extends above the roof line, common on flat-roof and Southwest-style homes. Cracks on top of parapets or at the roof joint are frequent leak sources.
Parapet cap
The covering on top of a parapet wall that keeps water from entering the wall. It may be stucco, flashing or another material.
Flat roof
A low-slope roof that looks flat but has a slight pitch to move water toward drains or scuppers. Flat roofs are common on Arizona homes and commercial buildings.
Low-slope roof
A roof with a gentle pitch, generally too shallow for standard tile or shingles without special underlayment or a different roof system.
Ponding
Water that stays on a flat roof long after rain, often defined as water still present 48 hours later. Repeated ponding can wear coatings and point to drainage problems.
SPF foam
Spray polyurethane foam, a liquid sprayed onto a roof that expands into a seamless, insulating layer. It must be protected by a coating because UV light breaks foam down.
Elastomeric coating
A flexible, rubber-like coating applied to flat and foam roofs that stretches and recovers as the roof heats and cools. Light-colored versions also reflect sunlight.
Acrylic coating
A water-based roof coating commonly used over foam and other flat roofs. It is usually white or light-colored to reflect heat.
Silicone coating
A roof coating known for resisting UV and standing water. It is often used on flat roofs where ponding is a concern.
Recoat
Applying a fresh layer of coating over an existing foam or coated roof before the old coating wears through. Timely recoats protect the roof surface underneath.
Chalking
A powdery residue that builds up on aging roof coatings as they weather. Heavy chalking means the coating is thinning.
Blister
A raised bubble in a roof surface caused by trapped moisture or air or a loss of bond between layers. A blister that breaks open can let water in.
Built-up roof
A flat roof made of several layers of asphalt and reinforcing felts, often finished with gravel or a coating. It is sometimes called BUR or tar and gravel.
Modified bitumen
A flat roof material made of asphalt blended with rubber or plastic modifiers and supplied in rolls. It is applied with heat, adhesive or self-adhering backing.
Single-ply membrane
A flat roof system made of large sheets of a single synthetic material, such as TPO or PVC. Seams are welded or sealed together.
TPO
Thermoplastic polyolefin, a single-ply membrane often used on commercial flat roofs. It is usually white and reflects sunlight.
Walk pad
A protective pad or path placed on a flat roof to protect the surface from foot traffic, especially around HVAC equipment.
Curb
A raised frame on the roof that supports equipment such as HVAC units, skylights or vents. The flashing around a curb must be sealed to prevent leaks.
Deck
The structural layer of a roof, usually plywood or OSB sheathing, that the underlayment and roofing are attached to. It is also called the roof deck or sheathing.
Decking
The sheets of plywood or OSB that make up the roof deck. Damaged or rotted decking is replaced during a re-roof.
Sheathing
Another word for the roof deck, the panels fastened to the rafters that support the roofing.
OSB
Oriented strand board, an engineered wood panel made from compressed wood strands and adhesive. It is commonly used as roof decking.
Rafter
One of the sloped structural boards that support the roof deck. Trusses do the same job in many newer homes.
Truss
A prefabricated triangular frame that supports the roof. Most newer homes in the Valley are built with roof trusses.
Square
The unit roofers use to measure roof area. One square equals 100 square feet of roof surface.
Pitch
The steepness of a roof, written as the inches of rise per 12 inches of horizontal run, such as 4:12. Pitch affects which roofing materials can be used.
Slope
The angle of a roof surface, often used interchangeably with pitch. Steeper slopes shed water faster.
Course
A single horizontal row of tiles or shingles running across the roof.
Exposure
The part of a tile or shingle that is visible and exposed to the weather after the next row is installed above it.
Tear-off
Removing the old roofing, and usually the underlayment, down to the deck before installing a new roof. It allows the deck to be inspected and repaired.
Re-roof
Replacing an existing roof with new roofing materials. It usually involves a tear-off and new underlayment.
Lift and relay
Removing the existing roof tiles, replacing the underlayment beneath them, and then reinstalling the same tiles. Broken tiles are replaced as needed.
Re-felt
Another name for a lift and relay, where the underlayment under a tile roof is replaced and the tile is put back. It is common on Arizona tile roofs because underlayment ages faster than tile.
Underlayment replacement
The process of renewing the waterproof layer under a tile roof, usually through a lift and relay. The goal is to stop leaks without replacing good tile.
Overlay
Installing new roofing over an existing layer instead of tearing it off. It is limited by code and by the condition of the existing roof.
Ridge vent
An exhaust vent that runs along the ridge of a roof and lets hot air escape from the attic. It works with intake vents lower on the roof.
Off-ridge vent
A low-profile exhaust vent installed near, but not on, the ridge. It is common on tile and shingle roofs in Arizona.
Turbine vent
A round, spinning exhaust vent that uses wind and rising heat to pull air out of the attic.
Soffit vent
An intake vent in the soffit that lets outside air into the attic. It must not be blocked by insulation.
Intake vent
A vent low on the roof, usually at the soffits or eaves, that brings outside air into the attic.
Exhaust vent
A vent high on the roof that lets hot, moist air leave the attic.
Attic ventilation
The flow of air through the attic from intake vents to exhaust vents. Good ventilation reduces attic heat and helps roofing materials last longer.
Radiant barrier
A reflective material installed in the attic, often on the underside of the roof deck, that reduces heat radiating into the attic. It works best in hot, sunny climates.
R-value
A measure of how well insulation resists heat flow. The higher the R-value, the better the insulation slows heat moving into the home.
Cool roof
A roof designed to reflect more sunlight and release absorbed heat more easily than a standard roof. Light colors and rated coatings and materials help keep cool roofs cooler.
Solar reflectance
A rating of how much sunlight a roof surface reflects, shown as a number between 0 and 1. Higher numbers mean a cooler surface.
Thermal emittance
A rating of how well a roof surface releases the heat it absorbs. It is one of the measures used to compare cool roof products.
Detach and reset
Removing solar panels or other rooftop equipment so roof work can be done, then reinstalling them. It is common during tile underlayment replacement and re-roofing.
Critter guard
A mesh barrier installed around the edges of solar panels to keep pigeons and other animals from nesting underneath.
Wind uplift
The upward force wind puts on a roof, which can lift or loosen tiles and shingles during monsoon storms. Proper fastening helps roofs resist it.
Monsoon season
The period from June 15–September 30 when Arizona sees sudden storms with high wind, dust, lightning and heavy rain. It is the most common time for storm damage to roofs.
ROC license
A contractor license issued by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors. Homeowners can look up a contractor's license status on the ROC website before hiring.

sections.h2: How to read these price ranges
sections.body:
The ranges on this page come from the overlap of several published sources, not the single highest or lowest number anyone printed. They are meant to help you plan, not to predict your exact bill. The full list of sources is at the bottom of the page.

Most roofing is priced by the square foot of roof surface or by the "square," which is 100 sq ft. Roof area is not the same as your home's living area. A 2,000 sq ft house often has 2,200–2,800 sq ft of roof once you count overhangs, patios and pitch, so a total based on living area alone will usually come in low.

Small jobs such as leak repairs are usually priced per job rather than per square foot. That is why the repair rows in the table show a per-job range and "Varies" in the total column.

sections.h2: What drives roof cost in Arizona
sections.body: Two homes on the same street can get very different numbers. Size and material set the starting point, and then the details of your roof move the price up or down. These are the factors the published sources point to most often.
bullets: Roof size and material: tile costs more per sq ft than shingle or foam. Larger roofs cost less per sq ft but more in total.
Pitch: a moderate pitch (5/12–8/12) adds roughly 10–20%, and a steep roof (9/12 and up) adds roughly 25–40%.
Height and access: two-story homes add roughly 15–25%. Tight access, multiple roof levels and rooftop AC units add labor.
Layers to remove: each extra layer of old roofing adds roughly $1,000–$3,000.
Complexity: hips, valleys, dormers, skylights and pipes all add labor and flashing.
Underlayment grade: often the biggest gap between tile bids. Premium synthetic or self-adhered underlayment adds roughly $0.40–$1.20 per sq ft over felt.
Tile condition: reusable tile lowers cost; broken, worn or discontinued tile raises it.
Hidden deck damage: rotted or delaminated plywood found after tear-off is billed per sheet or per sq ft.
HOA requirements: an approved tile profile or color can cost more and add approval time.
Solar panels: detach and reset typically runs $150–$300 per panel.
Coating system on foam and flat roofs: silicone costs more than acrylic, and proper thickness matters.
Permits: generally needed when the roof material changes and for many full replacements, typically $150–$500.
Season: some sources report summer heat surcharges of 5–10% or off-season discounts of 5–15%.

sections.h2: Tile underlayment replacement vs new tile
sections.body:
On most Valley tile roofs, the tile itself is not the part that wears out first. Concrete and clay tile commonly lasts 40–50 years or more, while standard 30-pound felt underlayment underneath usually lasts about 15–20 years in Arizona heat. When the underlayment fails, the usual fix is a lift and relay: the tiles come off, new underlayment goes down, and the same tiles go back on.

That is why underlayment replacement, at about $4–$7 per sq ft, costs noticeably less than a new tile roof at about $7–$12 per sq ft for concrete or $10–$18 per sq ft for clay. You are paying for labor and underlayment, plus a 5–10% allowance for tiles that break during handling.

New tile makes more sense when a lot of the existing tile is cracked or worn, when your tile has been discontinued and replacements can't be matched, or when your HOA or your own plans call for a different look. Upgraded underlayment such as 40-pound double felt, synthetic or self-adhered membrane costs more up front but is commonly rated for 20–40 years. Learn more on our tile roofs page.

sections.h2: Budgeting for foam roofs and coatings
sections.body:
Spray foam and coated flat roofs are less expensive to install than tile, but they come with a maintenance schedule you should plan for. The foam is protected by a coating, and in Phoenix sun that coating needs renewing about every 5–10 years. Acrylic coatings are commonly recoated every 5–7 years and silicone every 7–10 years.

A recoat on a 2,000 sq ft foam roof typically runs $3,000–$7,000, and smaller flat sections cost proportionally less. Putting a recoat off is usually the expensive choice: once UV wears through to bare foam, the damaged foam has to be repaired before a new coat goes on. Kept on schedule, published sources rate a foam roof at 20–30 years or longer.

Coatings over other flat roofs only work on a sound, dry surface. If the roof is worn, cleaning, repairs and primer can add about $0.50–$2 per sq ft. See our foam roofing and elastomeric coating pages for how each system works.

A repair makes sense when the problem is limited to one area and the rest of the roof still has life left. A few broken tiles, a lifted flashing or a single leak around a pipe usually falls in the $300–$1,500 range. Published ranges for replacing a section of tile underlayment run about $1,200–$2,800.

Replacement starts to make more sense when repairs keep coming back, when leaks show up in more than one place, or when the underlayment or shingles are near the end of their expected life. Paying for several repairs on a roof that is wearing out everywhere can cost more over a few years than addressing the whole roof once.

A good roofer should be able to show you what they found and explain which option fits your roof. Read more about repairs and maintenance and roof replacement.

sections.h2: How to budget for roof work
sections.body:
A realistic budget starts with your roof type and age and then adds room for the unknowns. These steps help you get to a number you can plan around.

  1. Know your roof. Note the material, roughly when it was installed and any past repairs.
  2. Think in roof area. Expect roof area to be larger than your living area.
  3. Start with the range. Use the table above for the main job, then check which add-ons could apply.
  4. Add a cushion. Decking damage and tile breakage often aren't visible until the old roof comes off, so set aside a contingency.
  5. Plan for the extras. Permits, solar detach and reset, and ventilation upgrades can each add to the total.
  6. Watch the calendar. Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30. Planning work before or after it gives you more scheduling room.

Financing is available for roofing projects. If you would like to spread the cost of a repair or replacement over time, ask about financing during your estimate and we'll walk you through the options.

It helps to decide on your scope first. Knowing whether you need a repair, an underlayment replacement or a full new roof makes it easier to compare a financed payment against your budget.
Published sources note that quotes for the same job can differ by $3,000–$5,000. Most of that gap comes from differences in what is included, not just in price.
bullets: Underlayment type and weight: felt vs double felt vs synthetic vs self-adhered.
What's included: tear-off, disposal, permits, flashing, ventilation and new drip edge.
Allowances: how decking and replacement tile are priced if they are needed.
Scope: whether the bid covers the whole roof, including patio covers and flat sections.
Licensing and insurance: confirm the contractor holds an active Arizona ROC license.

faqs: How much does a new roof cost in Phoenix?

Published Phoenix-area ranges put a new concrete tile roof at about $7–$12 per sq ft and an asphalt shingle roof at about $4.50–$7 per sq ft. For a 2,000 sq ft roof that is roughly $15,000–$24,000 for concrete tile and $9,000–$14,000 for shingles. Every roof is different, so an on-site estimate is the only way to know your cost.
How much does it cost to replace tile roof underlayment?

Most published Phoenix-area figures fall between $4 and $7 per sq ft, or about $8,000–$14,000 for a 2,000 sq ft roof. Premium underlayment and steep or complex roofs push toward the top. Every roof is different, and your actual cost can be more or less.
Why is underlayment replacement cheaper than new tile?

In a lift and relay, your existing tiles are reused, so you mainly pay for labor, new underlayment and a 5–10% allowance for broken tiles. A new tile roof adds the cost of all new tile. Every roof is different, so the gap between the two depends on your tile and roof layout.
What does a typical roof repair cost?

Most minor repairs, such as a few broken tiles, a flashing fix or a small leak, run about $300–$1,500 based on published Valley ranges. Leaks with hidden underlayment or deck damage often reach $1,500–$3,500. Every roof is different, so the cost depends on what is found.
How much does a paid roof inspection cost?

Published market ranges for a paid roof inspection in the Phoenix area run about $150–$450, and drone or infrared inspections can run up to about $600. Real estate and independent inspections are the most common reasons people pay for one. Every roof and situation is different. Integrity Roofing's inspections are a paid service; call 602-548-3770 for the current price.
How much does a foam roof recoat cost?

Published Phoenix-area ranges run about $1.50–$3.50 per sq ft, or roughly $3,000–$7,000 for a 2,000 sq ft foam roof. Silicone costs more than acrylic, and foam that needs repair before coating costs more. Every roof is different, so the condition of your foam matters.
How often does a foam roof need recoating in Arizona?

Published sources put the recoat interval at about every 5–10 years in the Valley, with acrylic coatings on the shorter end and silicone on the longer end. Staying on schedule protects the foam and avoids larger repair costs. Every roof is different, so have the coating checked as it ages.
Do I need a permit to replace my roof?

A permit is generally required when the roof material changes and for many full replacements, and published fees typically run $150–$500. Rules differ between Phoenix, Mesa, Gilbert, Chandler and Scottsdale, so check with your city. Every project is different.
How much does it cost to remove and reinstall solar panels?

Published figures run about $150–$300 per panel, or roughly $2,500–$6,000 for a typical 15–25 panel system. The work may include electrical disconnect, storage, new mounts and a separate permit. Every system and roof is different.
What hidden costs can come up during a re-roof?

The most common surprises are damaged decking, extra layers of old roofing and broken or unavailable tile. Decking is often priced at about $75–$150 per sheet installed, and each extra layer can add $1,000–$3,000. Every roof is different, so ask how these items are priced before work starts.
Is it cheaper to replace a roof in winter?

Some published sources report off-season discounts of 5–15% and summer heat surcharges of 5–10%, but this varies from roofer to roofer. Scheduling outside monsoon season (June 15–September 30) also gives you more flexibility. Every roof and schedule is different.
Why are roofing estimates so different?

Estimates for the same roof can differ by several thousand dollars because roofers include different underlayment, allowances and extras. Compare written, itemized estimates line by line rather than just the total. Every roof is different, so make sure each bid covers the same scope.
Do you offer financing for a new roof?
Yes, financing is available. Ask about it during your estimate and we'll explain the options. Every roof is different, so your estimate will reflect your roof's actual scope.
Are the prices on this page a quote?

No. These are estimated ranges gathered from published information from several Phoenix-area roofing companies and cost guides, and they are not a quote or offer from Integrity Roofing. Every roof is different, and actual costs can be more or less. Call 602-548-3770 to set up an on-site estimate.

It includes a roofing cost guide with estimated price ranges, in-depth guides on topics like tile underlayment and monsoon prep, a roofing FAQ with hundreds of answers, a glossary, roof type comparisons, a blog and a monthly newsletter.

sections.body:
We built this hub because homeowners kept asking us the same good questions: what a roof should cost, how long tile underlayment lasts, what to do after a monsoon and how to read an estimate. Rather than answer them one call at a time, we put the answers here so you can read them whenever it suits you.

Each resource has a different job. Some give a quick answer, others walk through a decision step by step. Start with whichever matches your question.

Our Roofing Cost Guide collects estimated price ranges for common roof work in the Phoenix area: repairs, tile underlayment replacement, new tile, shingles, spray foam, coatings and flat roofs. It also covers add-ons such as permits, decking, ventilation and solar panel detach and reset.

The ranges come from published information from several Phoenix-area roofing companies and cost guides, and every source is listed. Every roof is different, so use the guide for planning and rely on an on-site estimate for your actual cost.

The Homeowner Library holds our longer guides. They go deeper than a quick answer, covering how to hire a roofer, when tile underlayment needs replacing, how to prepare for monsoon season, how to read an estimate and how to handle a storm claim.

The library also includes a seasonal maintenance calendar, guidance on solar and roofing, attic heat and ventilation, flat and foam roof care, HOA approval and safe checks you can do from the ground. You'll find a list of trusted outside resources there too.

Our Roofing FAQ has hundreds of short answers to specific questions. It's the fastest way to look up something like how long a shingle roof lasts in Arizona, what causes a ceiling stain or whether slipped tiles are a problem.

Answers are written to be direct, and many link to a longer guide if you want the full picture.

sections.h2: Glossary, roof types and the blog
sections.body:
Roofing has its own vocabulary, and an estimate can be hard to follow if you don't know what a cricket, a valley or a drip edge is. The roofing glossary explains these terms in plain language.

If you're choosing a material, our roof type comparisons explain how tile, asphalt shingles, spray foam, coatings and flat roof systems differ in lifespan, upkeep and fit for Arizona heat. The blog covers timely topics, seasonal reminders and what we're seeing on Valley roofs.

Our monthly newsletter brings seasonal roof care to you. Expect reminders before monsoon season, tips for checking your roof after storms, and practical advice for keeping a roof in good shape through Arizona summers and winters.

Past issues are posted on the newsletter page, so you can read back through them at any time.

sections.h2: How to use the resource center
sections.body: Where you start depends on what's going on with your home. These paths cover the situations we hear about most.
bullets: Planning a re-roof: read the cost guide for estimated ranges, compare materials on the roof types page, then use the library guides on reading estimates and repair vs replace.
After a storm: start with the library's storm claim and monsoon guides, check what you can safely see from the ground, and call us if you see damage or a leak.
Buying a home: read about roof inspections and underlayment age, check the cost guide for the market range of a paid inspection, and look up unfamiliar report terms in the glossary.
Living in an HOA: read the HOA approval guide before you choose a tile profile or color, and ask your HOA for its approved product list early.

If you're buying a home, the roof is worth understanding before you close. Our guides explain what a roof inspection looks at and how to think about the age of the underlayment on a tile roof.

sections.body:
Each guide in this library tackles one topic in depth. Where our Roofing FAQ gives you a short answer, these guides explain the why behind it and walk you through the decisions you'll face.

Everything is written for homes in the Phoenix Valley, where intense sun, summer heat and monsoon storms shape how roofs age. The full list of guides appears below this introduction. Browse by topic or scroll the list to find what fits your situation.
The guides fall into a few broad groups. Most homeowners only need two or three at a time, depending on what's happening with their home.
bullets: Hiring and estimates: how to hire a roofer and how to read an estimate.
Tile roofs: tile underlayment, what it does and when it needs replacing.
Weather and storms: monsoon prep and storm damage claims.
Care and upkeep: the maintenance calendar, flat and foam roof care, and safe DIY checks.
Big decisions: repair vs replace, solar and roofing, and HOA approval.
Comfort and energy: attic heat and ventilation.

sections.h2: Hiring a roofer and reading estimates
sections.body:
Choosing a roofer is easier when you know what to ask. The hiring guide covers checking an Arizona ROC license, confirming insurance and understanding what a written estimate should include.

The guide to reading estimates explains common line items, such as underlayment type, tear-off, decking allowances, flashing and permits, so you can compare bids on the same terms. Pair it with our Roofing Cost Guide for estimated Phoenix-area ranges.

Most Valley homes have tile roofs, and the tile usually outlasts the underlayment beneath it. The underlayment guide explains what that layer does, how Arizona heat ages it, the warning signs of failure and how a lift and relay works.

It also covers the difference between underlayment types and when new tile might make more sense than reusing the old. See our tile roofs page for more.

Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30. The monsoon prep guide covers what to check before the storms arrive, from loose tiles and flashing to debris in valleys and drains on flat roofs.

The storm claim guide explains what to do afterward: how to look for damage safely from the ground, how to document it with photos and how the insurance process usually goes. For repair help, see our damaged roof page.

sections.h2: Maintenance, flat and foam roofs, and safe DIY checks
sections.body:
The maintenance calendar breaks roof care into seasons so small issues get caught before they grow. The flat and foam roof guide explains why coatings need renewing, how to spot ponding water and what a recoat involves. Learn more on our foam roofing and flat roofing pages.

The safe DIY checks guide lists what you can look at from the ground or from inside the attic, and what's best left to a roofer. Walking on tile can crack it, and roofs get dangerously hot in summer, so we keep these checks off the roof.

sections.h2: Repair vs replace, solar and HOA approval
sections.body:
The repair vs replace guide helps you weigh a targeted fix against a larger project, based on the roof's age, the number of problem areas and how often repairs have been needed.

If you have solar panels, the solar guide explains how they affect roof work and why panels may need to be detached and reset. The HOA approval guide covers working with your association on tile profiles, colors and timing so your project isn't held up.

In Arizona summers, a poorly ventilated attic gets extremely hot. That heat can shorten the life of roofing materials and make your home harder to cool. The attic heat and ventilation guide explains how intake and exhaust vents work together, signs your attic may be running hot and the common upgrades homeowners consider during a re-roof.

When a guide uses a term you don't know, the roofing glossary explains it in plain language. It's especially handy when you're reading an estimate or an inspection report full of words like underlayment, flashing, valley, cricket and square.

The library also points to outside resources that are useful when you're planning roof work. These include places like the Arizona Registrar of Contractors license search, where you can confirm a contractor's license, and your city's building permit office, where you can check whether your project needs a permit.

We include these so you can verify information on your own. Rules and requirements change, so always confirm the details with the source.

Guides can help you understand your options, but they can't see your roof. If you have a question about your home, call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

You can also visit the resource center for our cost guide, FAQ, blog and newsletter.

faqs: What is the Homeowner Library?

It's our collection of in-depth roofing guides written for Arizona homeowners. Each guide covers one topic, such as tile underlayment, monsoon prep or reading an estimate, in more detail than a short FAQ answer.
How are the guides organized?

The guides are grouped by topic: hiring and estimates, tile roofs, weather and storms, care and upkeep, big decisions like repair vs replace, and attic heat and ventilation. The full list appears below the introduction.

It depends on your situation. If you're planning a project, start with reading estimates and repair vs replace. After a storm, start with the monsoon and storm claim guides. For general upkeep, start with the maintenance calendar.
Do the guides include prices?
Price ranges are kept in the Roofing Cost Guide so they stay in one place and can be reviewed regularly. Every roof is different, so the only way to know your cost is an on-site estimate.
Are the guides specific to Arizona?
Yes. They're written for Phoenix Valley homes, with Arizona sun, summer heat and the June 15–September 30 monsoon season in mind.
Is it safe to check my own roof?

Some checks are safe from the ground or inside the attic, and our safe DIY checks guide lists them. We don't recommend walking on a tile roof or getting on any roof in summer heat; call a roofer instead.
What does the glossary cover?
The glossary explains roofing terms you'll see in estimates, inspection reports and our guides, such as underlayment, flashing, valley, cricket and square, in plain language.

The Arizona Registrar of Contractors offers a license search, and our outside resources list points to it. Integrity Roofing holds Arizona ROC #096629.
